Windows blocked the download, or called it a virus? That is a false positive: the build is not code-signed yet, so it starts from zero reputation. The FAQ explains how to check the file's hash yourself, and how to get it back.

title: What Is Kimi K3? A Complete Developer Guide for 2026
description: Recently, Kimi K3 was released by Moonshot AI. In this guide, we'll go over Kimi K3 specs, providers, and how to use it with OpenCode.
fullText:
Kimi K3 is Moonshot AI's newest open-weight model, and as of August 2026 the largest one anyone has released at 2.8 trillion parameters. It succeeds Kimi K2.7 Code, reads text, images and video natively, and holds up to 1,048,576 tokens in a single context window. Moonshot opened API access on July 16, 2026, then published the full weights on July 27.

Kimi K3 has some really impressive specs, especially for an open source model. Kimi K3 comes in with 2.8 trillion parameters. Models like GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.7 Code range from roughly 700 billion to just over 1 trillion. Its architecture provides Kimi K3 with 896 different experts when performing different tasks. It also boasts a context window of over 1,000,000 tokens. Kimi K2.7 Code had a context window of just 262,144, so K3 quadruples it. Kimi K3 supports text, images and video natively.

These stats were from Kimi K3's Hugging Face page.

Moonshot's Kimi K3 technical report credits its architecture and training changes, including Kimi Delta Attention, Attention Residuals and Stable LatentMoE, with roughly a 2.5x gain in overall scaling efficiency over Kimi K2.

Kimi's weights were released on July 27, 2026, as you can see in Kimi.ai's X post below.

On Moonshot AI's technical blog, they go through Kimi K3's benchmarks, which are on par with frontier proprietary models as well. Every number in this section comes from that blog. A few of them shifted slightly in the arXiv technical report, which was revised after launch, so it's worth checking both if a specific score matters to you.

Kimi K3 came in second to Claude Fable 5 on both tests, and both sets of numbers are the Python-tool-assisted runs. On CharXiv (RQ) with Python, Kimi K3 scored 91.3 against Fable 5's 93.5. On ZeroBench with Python, Kimi K3 tied GPT-5.5 at 41.0 against Fable 5's 46.0, while GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8 both landed below 40. That qualifier matters: without tool access, K3 drops to 84.8 on CharXiv and 23.0 on ZeroBench, where it ties Fable 5 rather than trailing it.

Kimi K3 is highly efficient at handling visual tasks. If your project needs agentic browser automation or anything else requiring computer vision, Kimi K3 is definitely worth a look.

Every first-party provider charges the same $3.00/1M input, $0.30 cached, $15.00/1M output as Moonshot itself. The only way to pay less is OpenRouter's cheaper routes, which start at $2.80/1M input and $14/1M output. Bear in mind that OpenRouter is a router, not a single price: its more expensive endpoints run to $6.00 input and $22.50 output, so pin your route if cost matters.

If you're looking to self host Kimi K3, you need a datacenter for best results. However, with a medium-sized pile of datacenter hardware, self hosting is possible. These numbers were collected by Kingy AI, which pulled most of them from vLLM's Kimi K3 recipe and the Hugging Face repo.

Buying that hardware outright is a high-six-figure decision. By our own math, eight B300s alone run about $424,000 at roughly $53,000 each, and a complete node lands somewhere in the $400,000 to $500,000 range once you add CPUs, NVSwitch fabric, networking, storage and the liquid cooling it requires. An AMD MI355X build comes in lower, closer to $250,000 to $350,000. Renting is far better documented: Kingy AI clocks 8x B300 at about $59 an hour, which is roughly $43,000 a month running continuously.

Practically speaking, you can host Kimi K3 with a "small" datacenter. The requirements above are the bare minimum to get the model working.

Those numbers all describe the full-precision MXFP4 checkpoint. Community quantization has since lowered the floor: Unsloth's 1-bit GGUF builds shrink K3 to about 594 GB, small enough for a high-RAM workstation or as few as four datacenter GPUs, at a real cost in accuracy. It's a way to poke at the model, not a way to serve it.

LinkedIn user Luke Mercado summed it up pretty well in the meme below.

If you're using it in production, you kind of need your own datacenter. You can read Moonshot AI's full technical report on arXiv: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence.

Now it's time to get started with Kimi K3 and OpenCode. We'll get started by installing via npm.

After you've installed, you need to log in to your model provider.

To give Kimi K3 web access, first we'll install the Firecrawl CLI.

Next, you can run setup mcp to configure an MCP connection.

The Firecrawl CLI will give you an option to select a number of environments like Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor and more.

When it's finished, relaunch OpenCode. Ask Kimi K3 if it can find the MCP.

The above methods ran into issues on Windows. However, OpenCode works just fine using WSL in Ubuntu.

One thing to know here, and it applies on every platform rather than just WSL: if you've already signed in with firecrawl login, firecrawl setup mcp will refuse to write your stored API key into a client config. That's a deliberate security rule, and the CLI tells you as much. You can either export FIRECRAWL_API_KEY into your environment yourself, or skip the problem entirely with the launcher, which configures the MCP and starts OpenCode with the key already in its environment.

Firecrawl launches OpenCode for us with the MCP server configured. Here, I prompt Kimi K3 to find the latest news.

Kimi K3 then finds the latest news using Firecrawl search. We get a variety of stories on politics, wars, elections and diseases. The search worked and our harness is good!

Perhaps one day the news will be good too.

Accessing Kimi K3 through various providers is easy. If you're calling Moonshot's hosted API directly, or a third party aggregator, you can get it up and running.

I will say that running OpenCode on native Windows is not so easy. As mentioned earlier, I ran into issues. My issue was an OpenCode bug where a crash leaves the terminal full of raw ANSI escape codes and a hidden cursor, forcing you to close PowerShell and start over. The issue is still open. If you're running OpenCode on Windows, use some form of WSL. It will save you from stress and headache.

Don't expect to run Kimi K3 locally without a Series A or some type of seed funding.

Kimi K3 is a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight multimodal AI model from Moonshot AI. It was released via API on July 16, 2026, with full weights published on July 27, 2026. It's the successor to Kimi K2/K2.7 and, as of August 2026, the largest open-weight model in the world. It's built for advanced reasoning, long coding, and agentic work.

K3 has 2.8 trillion total parameters with 104 billion active per token. It uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with 896 experts (16 active per token). It supports a 1,048,576-token context window, native multimodal input (text, image, video), and runs on Kimi Delta Attention with Attention Residuals.

K3 outscores both on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (60 vs. K2.7's 43 and GLM 5.2's 53) and leads coding benchmarks like ProgramBench and SWE-Marathon. GLM 5.2, however, is roughly 3x faster and cheaper per token, and ships with immediately available MIT-licensed weights, making it the better fit for high-volume, cost-sensitive coding work.

Weights are hosted on Hugging Face at moonshotai/Kimi-K3 (about 1.56 TB across 96 shards). API access is available through Moonshot's own platform (platform.kimi.ai, model name 'kimi-k3'), OpenRouter, and a variety of other providers.

Realistically, an enterprise GPU cluster. The weights run about 1.56 TB, which puts the practical floor at 8 accelerators with 288 GB each (B300, GB300 or MI355X) or a 16-GPU H200/B200 tier, though the 16-GPU tier leaves little room for KV cache and runs at heavily reduced context. Moonshot recommends supernode configurations with 64 or more accelerators for production. Consumer GPUs cannot run the full-precision checkpoint.

Like any other LLM, K3 has no live internet access on its own. To give it real-time web results, you need to connect it to an external retrieval tool such as Firecrawl, or any other harness that supports web access.

Firecrawl is an open-source context API that lets AI agents and LLMs search, scrape and interact with the web at scale. It helps convert messy websites into clean, LLM-ready Markdown or JSON. These formats can save drastically on token consumption compared to raw HTML.

Firecrawl's official MCP server exposes search, scrape, and interact tools to any MCP-compatible client (Claude, Cursor, VSCode and more). It can run keyless for quick testing, with an API key for production, or fully self-hosted for privacy. AI models like Kimi K3 can call endpoints like Firecrawl search mid-conversation to pull current information.

Firecrawl's free tier includes 1,000 credits/month (roughly 1,000 scraped pages or 500 searches) with no credit card required. This is a free tier, not a free trial. Teams can build software and upgrade their plan as needed.

VM doing ~50 IOPS when writing 2 lines of log per second

fullText:
PC; Replicant D6
This GoldenEye 007-styled retro shooter is an agreeable set of straightahead shooting missions that hark back to a simpler time, with simpler controls

With 007 First Light, 2026 has already given us the best James Bond game in more than three decades, since the release of Rare’s N64 classic GoldenEye 007. But what about those players whose loyalties lie not with the super-spy himself but the particulars of that 90s interpretation of his adventures?

Enter Agent 64: Spies Never Die. Made almost entirely by a single developer (who goes by the very cloak-and-dagger alias Replicant D6), its production values couldn’t be much further from the blockbuster First Light. There’s no voice acting, with all dialogue instead delivered via subtitles, while each location on your globe-trotting adventure is depicted by a repeating texture wallpapered over scenery so blocky you can count the individual polygons.

In lieu of any high-budget flash, Agent 64’s big special effect is nostalgia. From the title onwards, this retro shooter is one long homage to GoldenEye, and to its un-Bonded successor, 2000’s Perfect Dark.

Enemies have pinched facial features – a result of taking photographs of real people’s faces and wrapping them around diamond-shaped heads – and roll acrobatically from behind cover to take their next potshot, just as they used to. And yes, there’s a Big Head mode that swells those diamonds into enormous target-practice balloons.

Less explicably, Agent 64 retains the slightly strange control scheme of its inspirations, even though it doesn’t have to work around the (iconic but unwieldy) N64 pad that made it a necessity. You can pull a trigger for a zoomed-in precision aim, but somehow this is even fiddlier to steer with a modern analogue stick or mouse than it was back then. The first level features a pair of locks you must manually shoot; they remain the game’s toughest bosses.

Better by far to just run and gun, letting the generous auto-aim do its thing. OK, the target your gun seeks out might not always be the one you expected, or wanted, but playing this way unlocks a hectic pace of action that – nostalgic warmth aside – is Agent 64’s greatest asset.

It’s essential to the joys of split-screen deathmatch multiplayer, which generates the same kind of giggly fun that filled so many late 90s living rooms, especially once the match rules have been tweaked to allow only proximity mines or melee judo chops. (You can play online, but this is so counter to the elbows-on-the-sofa appeal of the thing that I never actually attempt it.)

Meanwhile, the story mode (which can be played solo or co-op with a partner) is so in hock to games of old that it ignores the subsequent 30 years of level-design knowhow. The number of dead ends and looping identical corridors can be infuriating, especially since dying means starting over from the beginning, but this is offset by the briskness of the missions. Each can be finished in less than five minutes, at which point the game will challenge you with a “par time” that often comes in under two minutes.

As you revisit these levels, trying to shave off vital seconds, their layouts begin to make much more sense. These are obstacle courses, really, where enemies aren’t so much a threat as they are something to be hurdled – or better yet, avoided. On top of this, Agent 64 piles hidden collectibles and challenge variants that recycle the levels in yet more ways, and their size makes them incredibly moreish.

The fantasy on offer here isn’t really being James Bond. It’s being young again, with one illicitly acquired copy of GoldenEye to last you the summer and all the time in the world to pick the cartridge clean. For all its rough edges, that’s a mission Agent 64 pulls off with aplomb.

Agent 64: Spies Never Die is out now, £19.64

title: ‘I feel like I’m at war’: are we losing the battle against machine-made music?
description:
Despite outcry from musicians, AI slop is creeping into the charts as record labels scramble to adapt to a new normal where hits can be made at the click of a button
This year, the battle for song of the summer has been eclipsed by a much more complicated – some would even say disturbing – debate. That’s because we find ourselves asking not “What’s the song of the summer?” but rather “Is the song of the summer even real?”
Among the top contenders for the title is Fenix Flexin’s Rubberz, a single released in June that has ascended to No 58 on the Billboard Hot 100 and racked up more than 35m Spotify streams. It’s not the sort of fare Fenix usually cooks up.
fullText:
This year, the battle for song of the summer has been eclipsed by a much more complicated – some would even say disturbing – debate. That’s because we find ourselves asking not “What’s the song of the summer?” but rather “Is the song of the summer even real?”

Among the top contenders for the title is Fenix Flexin’s Rubberz, a single released in June that has ascended to No 58 on the Billboard Hot 100 and racked up more than 35m Spotify streams. It’s not the sort of fare Fenix usually cooks up. The artist is known for his trap music as part of the rap duo Shoreline Mafia, but Rubberz is a mildly noirish, 80s-inspired synth-pop track featuring a voice nothing like his. The song has drawn comparisons to Morrissey, but it more closely resembles Men at Work’s Down Under, or a Weird Al Yankovic parody of Men at Work. It’s pretty awful. But more importantly, it has an uncanny quality to it. It sounds off.

Almost immediately after it came out, skeptics accused Fenix of employing artificial intelligence to create the track, if not entirely at least partly. He and the song’s credited producer, Purps on the Beat, initially denied it, with Fenix insisting that he’d just used Auto-Tune and a phoney British accent. The kerfuffle culminated this month when indie DJ-producer Medasin posted a video that he said proved that Rubberz had been made using the free generative music tool Treblo.

Medasin then captured himself giving Treblo prompts to pump out his own track. Its sound and lyrics were eerily close to those of Rubberz. Fenix rejected Medasin’s claims, posting what he said were clips of the song’s stems, or its fundamental components, but then Medasin posted a rebuttal of him demonstrating how AI songs, too, can be broken down into stems. A few days later, Fenix finally admitted to using AI to make Rubberz, writing: “never said I didn’t use AI, i said it had nun to do w recording process.”

This is in line with the findings of the platform’s own open-source classifier, Was This Made With Treblo?, which finds Rubberz to be “very likely Treblo” according to Wired. The tool hasn’t been independently reviewed, but the Treblo co-founder Ryan Tremblay confirmed to the Guardian that the classifier returns a very high probability score (“higher by far than any false positive”) for Rubberz, indicating that Treblo generated the song. “We built Treblo for everyone, from normal people experimenting at home to charting artists looking for new sounds,” Tremblay said. “Some artists appear to have used our model to find a sound that millions of people connected with, and that’s exciting.” When reached by the Guardian, Fenix’s representative declined to comment.

The uproar over Rubberz coincided with another major development in music in recent weeks. On 29 July, several record companies, including “the big three” – Universal Music Group, Sony Music and Warner Music Group – issued a proposal calling for global music charts to disqualify AI-generated tracks from consideration if they did not meet certain criteria. According to their suggested guidelines, a song could enter the charts only if it was properly authorized, lawful and substantially human-made, and does not raise concerns of streaming or chart manipulation. The issue, as the record companies stated in a press release, is that a significant number of AI-generated tracks hitting streaming services like Spotify have used tools trained on artists’ music without their consent and are often linked to fraudulently boosted streaming numbers. Under the proposed rules, these songs would not be allowed to enter charts such as the Billboard Hot 100.

At the same time, all the major record labels have announced partnerships with the likes of Nvidia, Spotify and Stability AI to develop AI music tools, with BMG announcing a partnership with the AI music-creation platform Suno this week. The rapper Tyga, a labelmate of Fenix, proudly told Vibe magazine recently that his new album $tarface was created with AI, saying: “There’s nothing wrong with using technology as a tool.” (The album received Pitchfork’s first 0.0 review in nearly two decades.)

He is not alone in his permissive attitude. While Rubberz is the first AI-generated single to crack the Hot 100, it is not the first to land on the Billboard charts. In November, the AI act Breaking Rust hit No 1 on the country digital song sales chart with Walk My Walk, a track credited to a person who goes by Aubierre Rivaldo Taylor. That same month, the AI-powered R&B singer Xania Monet – whose name instantly conjures actual human R&B singers Victoria Monét and Janelle Monáe – became the first AI act to enter a Billboard radio airplay chart, later climbing to No 1 on the R&B digital song sales chart. An avatar that the Mississippi poet Telisha “Nikki” Jones invented with Suno, she reportedly landed a multimillion-dollar record deal last fall.

After Xania Monet’s milestone, Billboard reported that a total of at least six AI-generated or AI-assisted artists had debuted on its various charts in 2025. The publication admitted, however, that the tally could be higher because it has become harder and harder to determine which songs have used AI, and just how much. This was validated a week later when a study by the French streaming platform Deezer and research firm Ipsos revealed that 97% of its participants couldn’t tell the difference between AI-generated music and human-made music.

Unsurprisingly, the proliferation of AI artists has struck a nerve with the human ones. SZA told i-D: “I feel like I’m at war because of AI.” Last month, she slammed AI generators like Suno and alleged that they were being trained on her songs without her permission. “If you’re a musician and you support this degenerate shit? You’re disgusting and there’s nothing you could ever say to me to make this OK,” she said. Jack Antonoff recently called AI-music makers “godless whores”. Billie Eilish, Bad Bunny, Kate Bush, Annie Lennox, Nick Cave, Sting, Stevie Wonder and Paul McCartney have all protested against the heavy use of generative AI in music.

And why shouldn’t they? Yes, dictating what one wants to create to an app requires a sliver of inspiration and imagination, but it pales in comparison with the blood, sweat and tears artists pour into music of their own – music that hasn’t been trained, often without permission, on reams of pre-existing copyrighted work. If those artists’ labor is grueling, the results, performed live and perfected in a studio by bands and session players with real instruments, can be deeply moving and totally exhilarating. Directing prompts to AI music generators like Suno, Udio and Treblo to spit out fully formed songs for mass consumption is a faster, cheaper, easier way to make music. It also disrespects and debases the art form, reducing hard-earned craft to half-assed mimicry.

If the outcry against AI sounds like a bunch of intransigent luddites shaking their fists at the inevitable arrival of a new era, know that naysaying artists and wary record companies are not alone. A recent report published by the music and entertainment insights company Luminate showed that listeners, especially members of gen Z and gen Alpha, are increasingly uneasy with AI-generated songs. The study found that 44% of US respondents felt less inclined to listen to a song if it involves generative AI. “Consumers are net negative,” a Luminate analyst told NPR in May. “People are more likely to feel uncomfortable than to feel comfortable with AI use.”

Universal, Sony and Warner are not demanding an outright ban on AI music from charts and streaming services. Though all three sued the AI music generators Suno and Udio in 2024, alleging they had trained their platforms on the labels’ artists without their permission, Universal settled with Udio and Warner settled with both Suno and Udio last year. (Sony has yet to settle with either.) The labels continue to work with Spotify and AI companies to develop generative music tools, in a move that effectively keeps their options open. Warner executive Robert Kyncl said the deals would foster “new creative and commercial possibilities”, adding: “Now, we are entering the next phase of innovation. The democratization of music creation.” Universal, Sony and Warner did not respond when approached by the Guardian for comment.

Meanwhile, other artists have expressed support of AI as a means to enhance songwriting. “With new technology, I try to use it as a tool to grow, not a crutch,” Björk wrote in a 2025 post on X. “If there is no soul in tomorrow’s music made by AI, it is because no one put it there … Anything that is mass-manufactured without the attention of creativity is that way, AI or not. So it is not about the tool – it is what you do with it.” Even McCartney enlisted AI to isolate John Lennon’s vocals for the final Beatles song, 2023’s Now and Then. What these labels and so many musicians want is a system of guardrails to ensure that AI use is limited, honest and transparent.

There is hope. In January, Bandcamp banned all music fully or substantially created by AI from the platform. Though Tidal allows fully AI-generated songs on its app if they are not linked to fraud or artist impersonation, they cannot collect streaming royalties or direct-to-fan sales revenue, and get tagged with an “AI” label. A coalition of music industry organizations, including the Grammys and the Recording Industry Association of America, recently announced that it was taking steps to notify listeners of AI use in recordings. This month, Spotify said that it would label AI artists with an “AI Persona” tag and exclude these artists from its personalized recommendations, while its optional “AI Credits” feature allows artists to note whether AI was used in a song’s creation.

Per the record companies’ proposed criteria, such AI Personas would not be chart-eligible. If Deezer’s findings are any indication, plenty of listeners would support this. Its 2025 survey results showed that 80% of respondents agreed that entirely AI-generated music should be clearly labeled to listeners, while 52% thought entirely AI-generated songs should not be included alongside human-made songs in the main charts.

Author and journalist CJ Farley echoed this sentiment in a recent column for Time. He dismissed the terms “AI artists” and “AI musicians”, suggesting that we instead refer to AI releases as “AI products”. Then he took it a step further, arguing that these products should be confined to their own chart “away from human musicians with real lives and with real financial obligations”.

If Rubberz is a joke, Fenix Flexin might have been trying to see exactly how much he could get away with. (That would at least explain why the song is such dreck.) But what about all the AI products with more nefarious purposes floating around out there undetected, the slop created by impostors and opportunists attempting to steal the work of others and pass it off as their own? There’s more at stake here than chart rankings. Artists’ livelihoods and legacies are on the line. If we don’t act now, tomorrow’s song of the summer may just be a sad, hollow shell of yesterday’s.

title: Are teens on ebikes the ‘new Hells Angels’? Not so fast, boomers
description:
Experts say better regulation is needed but that bad press about ‘motorized menaces’ puts the ebike revolution at risk
Beware, Americans: there’s a battery-powered threat cruising down beach paths, rolling up hiking trails and zipping along the streets of our cities.
By now, you’ve probably seen footage on social media of teens racing along streets, popping wheelies and weaving around car traffic with reckless abandon. The Los Angeles Times recently dubbed them the “new Hells Angels”. Other news outlets have referred to them as “motorized menaces” terrorizing communities. Sounds scary.
fullText:
Experts say better regulation is needed but that bad press about ‘motorized menaces’ puts the ebike revolution at risk

Beware, Americans: there’s a battery-powered threat cruising down beach paths, rolling up hiking trails and zipping along the streets of our cities.

In reality, these aren’t members of a federally designated violent criminal organization – they’re young adults riding electric two-wheeled vehicles: e-motorcycles, e-scooters and e-mopeds that have often been illegally built or modified to reach higher speeds than legal and regulated electric bicycles.

The proliferation of these vehicles is especially noticeable in fair-weather California, where mostly male riders have made headlines for dangerous antics and fatal crashes.

In May, Todd Spitzer, the Orange county district attorney, launched a specialized unit targeting “juveniles and adults, including parents who knowingly allow their children to ride illegal E-Motorcycles”.

That followed charges brought against parents earlier this year in the aftermath of crashes, including one in which a teen on an e-motorcycle fatally struck a pedestrian. In another case, a father was charged for modifying his 12-year-old son’s e-motorcycle to reach 60mph. The boy suffered serious injuries after he ran a red light and was hit by a motorist.

The media attention and government crackdowns extend beyond the Golden state. In New Jersey, the state legislature passed a law requiring registration, a license and, in some cases, insurance for anyone to ride an ebike. Similar laws are already on the books in a few other states, and comparable legislation has been proposed in others, including California and New York.

Look beyond some of the more hyperbolic headlines and you’ll see a familiar story about young people doing what they’ve always done: making dumb, dangerous decisions as they feel out the freedom of movement that grows with age.

That generational constant is happening as local and state authorities play catch-up with cheap, speedy vehicles that have flourished through mostly unchecked online retail sales. They are often marketed as ebikes, despite exceeding speed and power rules set for actual ebikes. Critics argue this makes it difficult for consumers to know the difference.

In this regulatory wild west, legal ebikes are caught in the crossfire. Experts, advocates and retailers say many officials are opting for scattershot over precise targeting to rein in illegal vehicles and invest in more education and infrastructure, putting the broader ebike revolution at risk.

The US and dozens of other nations experienced a surge in electric bike sales during the pandemic, as millions of people craved open space and movement in response to stay-at-home orders. People found an alternative travel mode for local errands, school drop-offs and work commutes, leaving behind the hassles that come with driving.

As components and batteries became cheaper to manufacture, new kinds of two-wheeled vehicles started to enter the market, many from China and often labeled as ebikes. Many of these vehicles had frames much more akin to motorcycles and dirt bikes than traditional bicycles. Another key difference: e-motos can go much faster, allowing riders to hit the same speeds as cars that many riders are too young to drive.

Ebikes are classified under federal law with specifics about their battery power – no more than 750 watts – plus rules about operable pedals to power the motor, and top speeds of 20mph for throttle bikes and 28mph with pedal assist only.

It’s these mis-marketed, cheaply made “junk” vehicles that have given real ebikes a bad rap, said Kendra Ramsey, director of the California Bicycle Coalition. Her organization advocates for policies that promote the benefits of riding bikes, including ebikes, and protect riders on the road.

“It is clear what an ebike is, but it’s not clear what it isn’t,” Ramsey said.

Biking advocates point to existing rules for actual ebikes and argue the majority of riders are not thrill-seeking speedsters but commuters who have tapped into ebikes’ convenience and low environmental impact as a replacement for local car trips.

Dillon Fitch-Polse, co-director of the BicyclingPlus research collaborative at the University of California, Davis, is concerned that authorities are responding to this “legal gray area” by adding bureaucratic barriers that will deter people of all ages from riding ebikes.

“That’s too bad, because either [riders are] going to do it illegally or they’re going to lose out on the freedom that an ebike can provide,” he said.

A better solution, Fitch-Polse said, would be to prohibit retailers from advertising these illegal bikes in the first place. There’s a bipartisan effort in California’s state legislature to do just that, which Ramsey’s organization is co-sponsoring.

The e-moto trend is also putting shops that sell legal ebikes in a bind, said retailer Brett Thurber. He and his wife own the New Wheel, with locations in San Francisco, Oakland and nearby Larkspur.

Thurber said kids and parents call his shops frequently or stop by in person seeking to buy e-motorcycles, which community-based businesses like his don’t sell. He uses those opportunities to educate people on the hazards of unregulated vehicles and preach the legal ebike gospel.

Though he’s made some converts, Thurber is sure many callers hang up and buy the e-moto they wanted online. As a longtime bike rider, he gets the appeal.

“Kids want freedom. They want something that’s cool,” Thurber said. “They like doing things that the adults kind of frown on and wag their fingers at.”

E-moto retailers have marketed that freedom with cheap, illegal vehicles just a few clicks away on Amazon, Walmart and other online platforms. A quick Amazon search revealed how easily consumers can purchase an e-moto, even if they’re seeking a street-legal ebike.

Typing “ebikes for teens” into Amazon’s search bar yielded dozens of vehicles that lack pedals and exceed the battery power of regulated ebikes.

The first sponsored result advertised a 2,000W dirt-bike style “Electric Bike for Adults [and] Teens”. The product description read: “Whether you’re climbing mountain trails or speeding through city streets, this ebike for adult [sic] delivers thrilling acceleration and reliable climbing power.”

Other listings contained similar mixed messaging. One “off road motorcycle” featured videos of young riders speeding and popping wheelies on public streets, which is illegal on this type of bike that is supposed to be registered in California as an off-highway vehicle.

“Safety is a top priority and we require ebikes sold in our store to meet applicable safety standards and Amazon policies. We are looking into the products in question,” a spokesperson for Amazon said via email when asked about those listings.

Amazon had previously announced it would stop selling electric vehicles in California that don’t comply with state laws. Some e-motos advertised on their platform now include a notice that “this item cannot be shipped to your selected address due to local laws or Amazon policy”, before advising would-be buyers to change the shipping address.

Ramsey said that lack of market regulation leaves a “big information gap” for parents, the majority of whom might not knowingly put their children in danger.

“A lot of adults are not in a good position to teach their kids good bicycling skills because they don’t ride bicycles themselves,” she said.

Some states and cities are beginning to crack down on these online markets. In April, Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, issued a consumer alert for “too fast, too furious” electric vehicles.

“Sometimes, what looks like an ebike or is marketed as an ebike is not a bike at all,” Bonta said. “Bike riders and parents: if your or your teen’s electric two-wheeled vehicle goes too fast, it might be a motorcycle or a moped – not an ebike.”

Earlier this month, New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, sent cease-and-desist letters to 42 retailers who sell illegal two-wheeled electric vehicles that don’t meet the city’s legal requirements for ebikes or scooters.

Unsurprisingly, as more people hop on both legal and illegal electric vehicles, more people are being hurt or killed. Researchers at UC San Diego analyzed California collision data from law enforcement agencies and found that ebike injuries increased “exponentially” from 2018 to 2024 and were “associated with a higher severity of injuries compared with traditional bicycles”.

Researchers noted that far more people on non-electric bikes were injured in crashes during the study period – more than 14 times as many compared with ebike riders. And the data is murky because e-motos “may be visually mistaken for ebikes and not be accurately identified by reporting agencies”.

But recent media coverage and public discourse about ebikes tend to miss a car-sized blindspot: the majority of crashes that kill ebike riders involve automobiles, according to federal data.

If you think it’s bad when someone operates a 50lb ebike recklessly, wait until you learn about how people drive around in 4,000lb cars, trucks and SUVs.

Ebike proponents worry the critical coverage of ebikes and e-motos could further obscure the fact that US roads are deadlier than nearly every other comparatively wealthy nation. And that’s driven by reckless behaviour of people behind the wheels of increasingly larger motor vehicles.

Recent data compiled by the US Consumer Product Safety Commission show 19 pedestrians were killed across the US in collisions with ebike riders in the eight years from 2017 to 2024. That’s roughly the average number of pedestrians killed by motorists every single day of 2024.

“It’s really sad to me that we have normalized so much traffic violence in society,” Fitch-Polse said. He argued public discourse and government officials take the easy route by pointing the finger at teenagers on trendy vehicles rather than reckoning with the systemic issues that make streets so dangerous in the first place.

For Thurber, the mounting toll of kids being hurt and killed while riding bikes represents “a societal failure”. He said authorities should address that not by stifling the autonomy that more kids and young adults have embraced through biking, but by redesigning streets to better protect them and other vulnerable road users from people behind the wheel of an automobile.

“My worry is that here … the tendency is to just put kids back in cars and have them be chauffeured around by their parents,” he said.

title: The Roots of Gekiga
description: What is Gekiga? And what are its roots?
fullText:
Children gathered to watch street kamishibaiOriginal 

Gekiga and Street kamishibai

　In terms of the development of Japanese manga after the war, the influence of "gekiga" (literally dramatic pictures, essentially graphic novels) cannot be ignored. In fact, from the 1960s to the 1970s, the emphasis on a more realistic style and subject matter aimed at a readership consisting of teenagers and older readers dominated the manga world, and the word "gekiga" came to be used in place of terms such as "story-based manga" and "manga". One of the roots of gekiga is street kamishibai (paper plays).

A kamishibai stage attached to a bicycleOriginal 

The word "kamishibai" initially meant paper-doll theater, but, in 1930, a style of kamishibai called "hirae", which involved drawing pictures on rectangular sheets of paper and then removing one at a time in order to tell a story, started becoming popular in Tokyo. So-called "kashimoto" (kamishibai dealers)—who produced hand-drawn kamishibai—loaned their kamishibai to performers called sellers who actually performed in the streets, and then the sellers sold sweets to children who showed up wanting to watch the kamishibai, which is how the business worked. According to a 1931 survey, there were already over 20 kashimoto in Tokyo alone at the time, and the popularity of kamishibai soon swept over the entire nation.

The Japan Educational Kamishibai Association "Chokorēto to Heitai" [Chocolate and Soldiers] (1939)Original 

Educational kamishibai and national policy kamishibai

 As a result of the popularity of street kamishibai, police and educators started viewing the vulgarity of its contents and expressions as a problem. At the same time, around 1935, the educational kamishibai movement—which involved creating and performing kamishibai suitable for children—was started in an effort to exploit the power of the medium to attract children. As the Second Sino-Japanese War dragged on, educational kamishibai—for which printed materials were distributed all over the country—started to include content aimed at helping the people understand Japan’s national policy. Many examples of this so-called "kokusaku kamishibai [national policy kamishibai]" were produced during the war.

"Bōken Katsugeki Bunko" [Swashbuckler Books], supplement of "Shonengaho Taizen" [Shonengaho Collection] supervised by Masayuki Honma (2015)Original 

Resurgence in popularity after the war

　After the war, street kamishibai once again started gaining popularity throughout the country. Its popularity even spread to boys’ magazines, and popular kamishibai writers were used for boy’s magazines. Major success stories include "Bōken Katsugeki Bunko [Swashbuckler Books]" (Meimeisha, currently known as Shonengahosha)—which serialized "Ōgon Batto [Golden Bat]", a work by Takeo Nagamatsu, the originator of the kamishibai boom starting in the 1930s—and "Omoshiro Book [Fun Books]" (Shueisha)—which serialized "Shōnen Ōja [Boy King]", a work by Sōji Yamakawa, who was already doing work for "Shōnen Club" (Dainippon Yūbenkai Kodansha) during the war.

Sōji Yamakawa, "Shōnen Ōja: Oitachihen" [Boy King: Background Story] ,Shueisha (1957)Original source: ©︎Soji Yamakawa

From kamishibai to emonogatari

 When the kamishibai performance style—which involved a kamishibaiya (kamishibai narrator) showing pictures drawn on rectangular sheets of paper and reading the sentences written on the back—shifted to magazines, the stories became "emonogatari" (illustrated stories), which had pictures drawn in frames with sentences to the side of them. The pictures used for street kamishibai were more realistic than those used for manga, and this style was used for emonogatari as well, but the layout of frames with pictures in them and sentences was not limited to Sōji Yamakawa’s relatively orthodox approach. Instead, there were a diverse variety of works, including works with unorthodox frame layouts, works with speech balloons, works without lines around frames, and works in which sentences were incorporated into frames.

Takeo Nagamatsu "Ōgon Batto" [Golden Bat], from "Bōken Katsugeki Bunko" [Swashbuckler Books], supplement of "Shonengaho Taizen" [Shonengaho Collection] supervised by Masayuki Honma (2015)Original 

Tetsuji Fukushima "Sabaku no Maō" [Demon king of the desert] reprint, volume 1, pp. 14-15Original source: ©Akitashoten 1949, 2012

Similarities between emonogatari and manga

 One major example of an early hit emonogatari, Tetsuji Fukushima’s "Sabaku no Maō [Demon king of the desert]" (Akita Shoten, 1949-56), actually resembled modern-day American superhero comics in its use of speech balloons, the shape and size of its frames as well as the free way these were changed, and the way each episode was printed in color. As a matter of fact, the editor of "Bōken-ō [Adventure King]" (Akita Shoten)—the magazine in which this work was serialized—bought up American comics from the occupation army and had Fukushima refer to them. This work is also famous for having a tremendous effect on Hayao Miyazaki when he was a boy.

Masahiko Matsumoto "Gekiga Bakatachi!!" [Gekiga Fanatics!!], pp. 6-7 (2009)Original source: ©︎Masahiko Matsumoto Courtesy of ebookjapan

Kashihonya and kashihon manga

　Kashihonya (booklenders) existed starting in the Edo period, but, after the war, they succeeded with an approach that involved renting out books and magazines for a rental charge without taking a deposit, and this business peaked throughout Japan from 1955 to 1964. One reason for this development was the publication of many manga books made specifically for kashihonya. Even though kashihon (rental book) manga were criticized for their vulgarity, they expanded the range of the manga market, and they represented an attempt to tackle subject matter and expressive ideas that were not present in manga published in magazines for boys and girls. Therefore, the role they played in terms of the development of manga after the war cannot be ignored.

Sanpei Shirato "Ninja Bugeichō" [History of the Ninja Arts], volume 7, pp.98-99 (1997)Original source: ©︎Sanpei Shirato,Tetsuji Okamoto / SHOGAKUKAN

From kamishibai to kashihon manga

　The world of kashihon manga included Shigeru Mizuki, Sanpei Shirato, and others who switched their jobs from street kamishibai as it began to decline from 1955 to 1964. Genres such as historical stories with graphic depictions of events as well as horrific ghost stories show the depth of the relationship between street kamishibai and kashihon manga. Sanpei Shirato’s Ninja Bugeichō [History of the Ninja Arts] (Sanyōsha, 1959-62)—a sweeping historical drama set during the Sengoku Period that depicts the chaotic interactions between Sengoku warlords such as Nobunaga Oda, a ninja group known as the shadow clan that leads a hyakushō ikki (peasant revolt) against them, swordsmen who have noticed the inconsistencies inherent in their hierarchical class society, and others—gained a lot of support from young people of the day, partially due to the fact that there were a lot of student and social movements at the time.

Sanpei Shirato "Ninja Bugeichō" [History of the Ninja Arts], volume 7,Sanyōsha (1960)Original source: -

Yoshihiro Tatsumi "Gekiga Hyōryū" [A Drifting Life], volume 2, SerinKogeisha, pp. 204-205 (2008)Original source: ©︎Yoshihiro Tatsumi

The birth of gekiga

　Kashihon manga included many historical stories, detective stories, ghost stories, and other works for which a readership consisting of teenagers and older readers was assumed, many of whom were not satisfied by the manga in magazines for boys and girls. Yoshihiro Tatsumi—who was working at Hakkō, an Osaka-based kashihon manga publishing company at the time—dubbed more realistic, dramatic story-based manga for such readers "gekiga". In 1959, he formed the "Gekiga Kōbō" (Gekiga Studio) with Takao Saitō and other like-minded colleagues working at the same publishing company and then sent a message entitled the Gekiga Studio Notice to newspaper and publishing companies, thereby spreading the gekiga name.

Title page of "Gekiga Primer" from "Weekly Shōnen Magazine", January 1, 1970 issue, Kodansha (1970)Original source: ©︎Takao Saito / Saito production

From kashihon manga to magazines

　In 1959, "Weekly Shōnen Magazine" (Kodansha) and "Weekly Shōnen Sunday" (Shogakukan)—the first weekly magazines for boys—were established. In the late 1960s, the works of popular kashihon manga writers were used one after another for both magazines, and "Weekly Shōnen Magazine"’s emphasis on gekiga in particular brought the publication success, resulting in a circulation of over one million copies. From the late 1960s to the early 1970s, numerous manga magazines aimed at young men were established, and gekiga—which dominated manga magazines for boys as well as young men—entered its golden age. "Weekly Shōnen Magazine"’s "Gekiga Primer", which was planned by Shōji Ōtomo for the leadoff articles and focused on Takao Saitō’s "Muyōnosuke", is arguably a symbol of this.

"Gekiga Primer" from "Weekly Shōnen Magazine", January 1, 1970 issue, Kodansha (1970)Original source: ©︎Takao Saito / Saito production

Shigeru Mizuki "Hakaba Kitarō" [Kitarō of the Graveyard], volume 1 (kashihon manga reprint) (2006)Original source: ©︎ Mizuki Production, KADOKAWA

Shigeru Mizuki

　GeGeGe no Kitarō, one of Shigeru Mizuki’s representative works, started out as "Hakaba no Kitarō" [Kitarō of the Graveyard] (1954)—which was drawn by him while he worked on street kamishibai in Kobe in response by advice to make something like "Hakaba Kitarō" (written by Masami Itō and drawn by Tajimi Kei in 1933), a hit street kamishibai from before the war. (Apparently, Mizuki himself never actually saw "Hakaba Kitarō" before the war.) From 1960 to 1964, Kitarō appeared in kashihon manga released by various publishing companies, and, in 1965, Weekly Shōnen Magazine started publishing "Hakaba no Kitarō" on an irregular basis. Starting in 1967, the work was serialized with a new title: "GeGeGe no Kitarō". Kitarō’s character gradually became more approachable during the transition from kashihon manga to Weekly Shōnen Magazine.

Text: Hirohito Miyamoto（Meiji University）

title: Ukrainian drones wipe out US tank brigade in live war game
description: Ukrainian drone pilots teach the US military and NATO hard battlefield lessons.
fullText:
Ukrainian drone teams demolished a brigade of US Army tanks and armored vehicles during a live war game held this year—but the US soldiers were lucky enough to get “respawn” attempts while learning from the experience.

The semiannual military exercise, called Combined Resolve, gave the US military a firsthand taste of how modern drone warfare has evolved on the battlefields of Ukraine. The Ukrainian drone operators participating in the exercise were easily able to spot and destroy US armored vehicles by mimicking the actions of dropping bombs from above or moving close enough to simulate a kamikaze strike, according to US officials and a participant who spoke with The Wall Street Journal.

US armored vehicles were being destroyed so quickly that they were “respawned” and sent back into the simulated fray, a US official told The Wall Street Journal. The US troops who participated in the exercise—held in Germany from April 9 to May 10—were on rotational deployment from Fort Hood, Texas.

“Using the drones with the Army, it keeps everyone on edge,” according to an unidentified US Army soldier in a promotional video for Combined Resolve. “There is never a safe spot or safe moment in the game anymore.”

The participating troops hailed from the 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team of the 1st Cavalry Division, which typically operates armored vehicles, like M1A2 tanks and Bradley infantry fighting vehicles.

But by repeating the training scenario throughout the two-week exercise, US Army troops got better at figuring out how to disperse and hide from the drones while using countermeasures such as electronic warfare.

The US military is not alone in learning such lessons from battle-hardened Ukrainian drone operators.

Ukrainian drone teams also participated in a Swedish-led military exercise for NATO, called Aurora 26, that was also held in May. A mock mechanized assault by NATO tanks and infantry fighting vehicles allowed Ukrainian drones to take out dozens of the attacking armored vehicles, which eventually forced planners to reset the war game, The Kyiv Independent reported.

Armored tanks first played a useful role in helping break through entrenched battlefield lines during the final years of World War I more than a century ago. But since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, frontline combat has seen the return of positional warfare centered on fortified networks of trenches. That is because the increased lethality of modern drone warfare has largely negated large assaults by armored vehicles and troops in recent years.

The current lethality of the so-called drone kill zone has forced both sides to rely primarily on infiltration tactics using small groups or even individual soldiers when trying to take or reclaim territory, sometimes riding motorcycles, all-terrain vehicles, or horses. Russia’s offensives, which are aimed at seizing more Ukrainian territory, have been reduced to bloody attritional operations where soldiers are sent forward on near-suicidal missions in what Russians themselves describe as the “meat grinder.”

Meanwhile, armored tanks and vehicles have mostly become an endangered species on the frontlines. Russia has lost more than 14,000 tanks and armored vehicles of other types during the war, according to the Dutch open source intelligence tracking project Oryx, which only counted visually verified losses. Ukraine has lost over 6,000 armored combat vehicles.

But both Russia and Ukraine are still attempting to use mechanized assaults with vehicles on occasion. In May of this year, Ukraine used armored vehicles in limited counterattacks that penetrated Russian defenses—the result of Ukrainian military experiments with using electronic warfare and targeted strikes on Russian drone pilots to help achieve localized territorial gains. That was a notable feat, given that enabling mechanized vehicles to survive the Russian drone kill zone was “categorically impossible in 2025,” according to the Institute for the Study of War based in Washington, DC.

In July, Russian forces launched their own mechanized assault with tanks and infantry fighting vehicles in the hotly contested Donetsk Oblast in eastern Ukraine. This attack was apparently repelled, with the Ukrainian military reportedly destroying 80 percent of the Russian vehicles before they even reached the frontlines.

The Pentagon has requested more than $54 billion for acquiring drone and counterdrone systems in its fiscal year 2027 budget proposal, an amount that exceeds Ukraine’s entire military budget. But as the Combined Resolve exercise showed, the US military must also adapt its unit training and operational practices to the threat of short-range drones if it wants troops to survive on future battlefields.

title: Trump Promised To End Foreign Aid. Now He's Giving Christian Groups Nearly $2 Billion. (opinion)
description: The administration says faith-based organizations deliver aid more efficiently, but offers no data to support that claim—and its preference for religious providers raises constitutional questions.
fullText:
The U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) may be dismantled, but billions of taxpayer dollars are still flowing overseas.

Last week, the Trump administration announced that it will direct nearly $2 billion in humanitarian funding toward faith-based organizations, including $1.4 billion through its America First Global Health Strategy. Three Christian organizations—World Vision, Compassion International, and Samaritan's Purse—are among the largest recipients, with the State Department calling it "the largest allocation of global health foreign assistance to faith-based organizations in over 20 years."

Of the nearly $2 billion, $850 million will go to a World Vision-led global consortium, $570 million to faith and community-based health facilities through foreign governments, $300 million to Samaritan's Purse, and $238 million to a World Vision and Compassion International humanitarian consortium.

Samaritan's Purse, which will receive the funding over two years, explicitly describes itself as an "evangelical Christian organization" that provides "spiritual and physical aid." Its mission statement says it helps "meet the needs of people…with the purpose of sharing God's love through His Son, Jesus Christ" and "the organization serves the Church worldwide to promote the Gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ."

This is not the first time the group has received federal money. From 2021 to 2025, Samaritan's Purse was awarded $90 million from USAID, according to the Brookings Institution. Still, it has faced its share of controversies over the years.

The organization requires employees to oppose same-sex marriage, and its CEO, Rev. Franklin Graham, has faced criticism for some of his statements on gay issues and Islam. This includes social media posts saying, "We should stop all immigration of Muslims to the U.S." and "Every Muslim that comes into this country has the potential to be radicalized." Graham is also an ally of President Donald Trump and defended the president after he created an AI-generated image depicting himself as Jesus in April, supporting Trump's claim that "he thought it was a doctor."

Its "Operation Christmas Child" initiative—which sends shoeboxes full of toys and treats to impoverished children worldwide—has been criticized for sending Christian missionary messages to Muslim countries in the hope of converting poor children. "Angella received an Operation Christmas Child shoebox filled with presents last year at this time," the charity's website reads. "Since then, she's led her Muslim family to Christ."

In 2025, MinistryWatch downgraded Samaritan's Purse from "Give with Caution" to "Withhold Giving" after the organization left the Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability because it did "not meet board composition recommendations," according to MinistryWatch.

World Vision, which will lead a consortium eligible for up to $850 million over five years, also describes itself as a "Christian charity" that partners with "pastors and Christian leaders throughout the world." They aim to "strengthen local churches…to support sustained spiritual and physical transformation." Likewise, Compassion International "partners with local churches in impoverished communities" to introduce "vulnerable children to Jesus as [they] meet their critical needs."

While these charities may provide valuable humanitarian assistance, it is unclear why American taxpayers should be compelled to finance their work. What's equally baffling is the administration's seeming insistence that foreign aid go only to Christian groups.

Through the America First Global Health Strategy, the State Department is mobilizing $1.4 billion in country-specific grant programs. The State Department's official Q&A for its Nigeria global health funding makes its preference for religious organizations explicit: "there should be a priority placed on engaging local Nigerian organizations with a strong emphasis on faith-based and community-based providers."

Similarly, in the Ivory Coast, the State Department has made sustaining "Integrated Service Delivery in Faith- and Community-Based Facilities" one of four explicit objectives. Applicants are told to place a "strong emphasis on faith-based and community-based providers." The department also envisions a direct role for religious institutions in delivering public health programs, including "the involvement of places of worship supporting maternal and child health week."

The State Department claims that faith-based organizations spend taxpayer money more efficiently than secular groups and that their efforts reach frontline communities better. The department does not, however, provide supporting data or a methodology for those figures in its announcement, and there is no reason to believe that faith-based NGOs are any less wasteful than nonreligious organizations.

Prioritizing faith-based organizations for federal funding could also pose a constitutional problem. Under the First Amendment's Establishment Clause, the government is prohibited from taking  "actions that unduly favor one religion over another," according to the Legal Information Institute. It also prohibits "the government from unduly preferring religion over non-religion, or non-religion over religion." While it is unclear whether this funding round violates the Constitution, the State Department's guidance does explicitly prioritize faith-based providers' access to taxpayer dollars.

"The administration is openly restructuring American foreign assistance around religion," said the Freedom From Religion Foundation Copresident Annie Laurie Gaylor in a press release. "Taxpayers should not be forced to bankroll an administration's campaign to elevate and subsidize religion."

The Trump administration promised to cut wasteful overseas spending, but replacing one type of ideologically motivated spending with another is hardly a victory for taxpayers.

The post Trump Promised To End Foreign Aid. Now He's Giving Christian Groups Nearly $2 Billion. appeared first on Reason.com.

title: Yale seismologist Maureen Long says recent earthquake surge is normal
description: Scientists record about half a million earthquakes strong enough to be felt by instruments every year, Long says.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — A recent string of major earthquakes in recent weeks, including a 7.4-magnitude quake that triggered a dramatic rescue of a baby in Colombia, has left many wondering whether the events are connected. According to Yale seismologist Dr. Maureen Long, they're not, and the frequency isn't out of the ordinary.

"This is a question that I get from family and friends all the time," Long told NewsNation's Jesse Weber. "The short answer is yes; this is normal."

Long said roughly half a million earthquakes strong enough to register on scientific instruments happen every year. For quakes of magnitude 7 or higher, the average is between 15 and 18 annually, though that number can vary year to year.

Long, who researches seismic activity in the Pacific Northwest and eastern U.S., also flagged an earthquake risk she says the public underestimates: the Cascadia subduction zone off the Pacific Northwest coast. The zone produced a magnitude 9 earthquake roughly 300 years ago, and Long said another is inevitable.

"It's really important for us to continue doing scientific research into what exactly that magnitude 9 might look like in the future and how applying that scientific knowledge so that we can be prepared for it," Long said.

Scientists still cannot predict earthquakes with the accuracy used to forecast hurricanes, though researchers are working to improve early-warning capabilities.

fullText:
Emergency teams in Colombia are searching desperately for survivors of an earthquake that has killed at least 273 people as the crucial window for rescues drew to a close on Thursday, with the government still only accepting help from a handful of countries.

Nearly 380 people are still missing, Colombia's agency for disaster preparedness and response said Thursday, after the quake damaged homes, schools, bridges and airports across a large swathe of the country.

"Our main efforts are focused on the missing," said President Abelardo De la Espriella in a statement late Wednesday, calling for unity.

Monday's devastating earthquake, the worst to hit Colombia in decades, posed an early test for the newly inaugurated leader. His government has surprised some by turning down or limiting help from several countries in the region, after they offered immediate assistance following the 7.4 magnitude quake.

On Wednesday, the newly appointed head for the disaster preparedness and response agency said the government would request rescue teams from only four countries: the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel. In Colombia's view, only those countries' rescue teams have the international and national certifications required for the job, said National Unit for Disaster Risk Management director David Tamayo Roldán.

Organizations including the United Nations and Mexico's famed "Topos" rescue brigade initially said they had not received a request for help with search and rescue. Aid agencies warn there is a critical 72-hour window after which the possibility of finding anyone alive in the rubble of collapsed buildings drops dramatically.

The Colombian Foreign Ministry has said it was preparing a list of "specific needs" to request international aid and that it had asked the United Nations Development Programme to provide support. In a statement, Foreign Minister Omar Bula also said that Colombia has "not excluded absolutely any country in terms of the offers that have been made to us," adding, "We work with countries without any ideological or political consideration."

Political scientist Sandra Borda linked the difficulties to the tense political transition between the current and previous administrations and said the new government showed "a deep distrust of some parts of the international community," which she considered "difficult to understand."

She added that there was "no clarity about the procedure that was to be followed."

"There was a perception from the beginning that the rescue teams would be sufficient, although a technical assessment was never made public to confirm that they would indeed be enough to deal with all the damage and destruction caused by the earthquake," she said.

It has also been unclear where international personnel are needed. The emergency chief of the fire department in Cali, one of the most affected cities, warned volunteers not to approach collapsed sites "because there are already enough specialized personnel to carry out the rescue work without complications."

The Topos Tlatelolco Rescue Brigade, a Mexican group with extensive experience responding to natural disasters, said Wednesday that Colombian authorities "will not allow the entry of external rescue groups" because the work is being handled by national rescuers.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed that her government was in contact with Colombia, but said its government had not given its approval to rescuers, who were "ready to leave at any moment."

"We are sending, via Hercules planes, food supplies, medical supplies, and other things they've requested. But yes, just to clarify: the rescue brigade from the Secretariat of National Defense was not approved by the Government of Colombia," she said.

Meanwhile, in Pereira, one of the most severely affected cities, the foreign ministry celebrated the arrival of 19.5 tons of aid from Mexico.

"Additional flights are expected in the coming days. Colombia is not alone! The international community is with us," the ministry said on X.

Michael Rios contributed to this report.
