title: Forget left vs. center. Democratic voters are making clear they just want change
description: Democrats remain mixed over what ideological direction the party should take.  In marquee Senate primaries in Michigan and Minnesota, progressive candidates defeated two members of Congress with signi...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats remain mixed over what ideological direction the party should take. But across a series of closely watched primaries, they are sending a clearer message about the party's path forward: They want change.

In marquee Senate primaries in Michigan and Minnesota, progressive candidates defeated two members of Congress with significant backing from party leaders. Wisconsin voters narrowly rejected a democratic socialist but still chose a 40-year-old county executive who is seeking to become the state's first Black governor. And in Connecticut, voters ousted one of the longest-serving Democrats in Congress for a challenger who campaigned on generational change.

The results so far this month deliver no clear ideological mandate. Instead, they add to mounting evidence from this year's primaries of a Democratic appetite for turnover that is cutting across the party's traditional divisions.

"The through line between these races isn't ideology. It's impatience with this political system that feels disconnected from the urgency voters feel," said Lis Smith, a national Democratic strategist. "The demand for change is much broader than the demand for socialism."

The immediate challenge for Democrats is whether they can harness the frustration fueling revolts against their own party and turn it against Republicans in November. Beyond that looms the 2028 presidential race, when a new generation of leaders will compete to shape a changing Democratic Party.

"If leaders in our party don't recognize that we need to make changes, then the changes are going to come from the ground up," Luke Bronin, a former mayor who defeated 14-term Connecticut Rep. John Larson in Tuesday's primary, said in his victory speech. "That's a message our party needs to hear."

Progressive leaders touted Tuesday's results as further proof that their message is working after victories in Minnesota and Michigan.

"What we are seeing is that people are sick and tired of establishment politics and establishment policies," Sen. Bernie Sanders told The Associated Press on Wednesday, pointing to a string of progressive victories around the country.

In Wisconsin, Democratic socialist Francesca Hong had hoped to also ride the wave of recent progressive victories to the Democratic nomination for governor. Instead, she narrowly lost to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a more moderate Democrat who had the backing of outgoing Gov. Tony Evers.

Hong's defeat also came after a number of her past comments resurfaced, including support for defunding the police and a call to cancel Thanksgiving, which she said was a joke. Unlike El-Sayed, Hong didn't receive the backing of some of the nation's most prominent progressive leaders, including Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Sanders said Wednesday that he didn't endorse Hong because his team lacks the resources to "get involved in every single race. Period. And that's about it." He nevertheless praised her "very strong grassroots campaign" for getting "a whole lot of people excited."

The result illustrates a tension for the party's ascendant left flank. Candidates running on populist economic messages have found growing success with Democratic voters. But some positions associated with the progressive movement's recent past remain vulnerabilities — particularly among voters worried about electability in November.

"A lot of Democrats are traditionalists on things like culture issues. This is not about culture, it's about economics. It's about corruption," said David Axelrod, who was an adviser to President Barack Obama. "The closer that candidates hew to those issues, the larger the base they're going to be able to accumulate."

That tension was evident Tuesday for Sarah Atkins Hoggatt, 61, who said she agreed with Hong on some issues but worried that Hong's deeply progressive politics and the democratic socialist label would make it harder for her to defeat Republican Tom Tiffany. She voted for Crowley.

"I didn't vote my heart," Atkins Hoggatt said.

Progressives scored a much clearer victory in Minnesota, where Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan resoundingly defeated centrist Rep. Angie Craig. Craig had the backing of House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other prominent Democrats, while Flanagan was supported by Sanders and Sen. Elizabeth Warren.

Flanagan, similar to El-Sayed in Michigan, highlighted her opponent's support from wealthy donors while also attacking her vote for a Trump-backed immigration bill that became a liability after immigration agents shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.

As in Michigan, the winning progressive candidate was significantly outspent.

"Super PACs spent over $80 million trying to defeat El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan," Sanders said. "They lost both elections. I think what people are saying is, we're sick and tired of billionaires and their super PACs buying elections."

Flanagan is 46 years old. Crowley is 40. And El-Sayed is 41. But nowhere was the demand for generational change more explicit Tuesday than in Connecticut.

Bronin, 47, defeated the 78-year-old Larson — who was first elected to Congress in 1998. A central theme of Bronin's campaign was the need for a new generation of leadership in Washington.

Larson became the seventh Democratic House incumbent to lose a primary this year, many of them to younger challengers. The defeated incumbents and the Democrats replacing them span ideological lines, making the wave of losses difficult to explain simply as a shift to the left.

The push for generational turnover has taken on greater urgency since 2024, when concerns about President Joe Biden's age ended his reelection campaign and forced Democrats into a reckoning over aging leadership.

That sentiment was evident among voters in Larson's district. Dan Schnaidt, a 73-year-old Democrat, said he appreciated Larson's service but believed it was time to move on.

"It's time for new blood, for new ideas," Schnaidt said.

While Hong fell just short in Wisconsin, the strength of her insurgent campaign highlighted another force reshaping Democratic politics: younger voters.

Cody Chandler, a 35-year-old software engineer, voted for Hong and called her "probably the most exciting candidate I've seen." Unlike in elections past, Chandler said, he voted for the candidate he most wanted to win rather than the one he considered most electable.

That support showed up geographically. Hong won Madison, home to the University of Wisconsin's flagship campus, by nearly 7 percentage points, though it wasn't a big enough of a margin to help her win the nomination.

A similar pattern helped propel El-Sayed to victory a week earlier in Michigan.

El-Sayed won Washtenaw County, home to the University of Michigan, by nearly 25 percentage points and Ingham County, home to Michigan State University, by 23 points. He also won Grand Rapids, with its large population of younger, college-educated voters, by nearly 26 points.

Jordan Snyder, a 20-year-old Michigan voter who supported El-Sayed, said she backed him because of his progressive positions and because she viewed him as someone she could trust, rather than "someone who I feel could be bought and sold."

"People are feeling like a lot of the people that they've trusted that have been in government haven't really been living up to expectations," Snyder said.

title: Here’s What to Do Now That Microsoft Edge Is Phasing Out Ad Blockers
description: An alternative browser may be in your future.
fullText:
If you're a Microsoft Edge user, you will soon find that some older extensions—like uBlock Origin—no longer work. That's because Microsoft is following Google Chrome's lead in transitioning to the Manifest V3 extensions platform and disabling MV2 add-ons in the process. Edge is built on Google's Chromium engine, so the change isn't unexpected, but it does impact users who rely on older ad blockers.

Microsoft recently announced that it will begin turning MV2 extensions off by default over the next few months, and support for these add-ons will end completely for most users by the close of 2026. (The transition for enterprise is expected to be finalized in early 2027.)

Microsoft notes that 95% of MV2 extensions on Edge have already moved to MV3, leaving fewer than 60 in the Edge Add-on store still on MV2. That includes uBlock Origin, which does have an MV3 version in uBlock Origin Lite, but the latter isn't as powerful as its predecessor and hides content rather than keeping it from loading in the first place. AdBlock, AdBlock Plus, and AdGuard are other MV3 alternatives with Edge versions, though they are not perfect replacements for uBlock Origin either thanks to restrictions on how MV3 ad blockers are able to filter content.

If you want to retain the ad-blocking features you're used to, you can move away from Edge (and Chrome) to a browser that's not Chromium-based. The alternatives also tend to be pretty decent when it comes to privacy. One is Firefox, which runs on its own Gecko engine and still allows these older ad-block extensions, including uBlock Origin. DuckDuckGo and Brave both have built-in ad-blocking capabilities. Note that Opera, which is Chromium-based, has said the platform plans to continue MV2 support for now, but that may end eventually.

title: USAID fallout: In Nepal, when the aid workers stopped coming, the women and babies started dying
description: The young mother’s breath had grown ragged.  Inside her mud home in rural Nepal, she hunched over in agony, pain pummeling her pregnant belly, her swollen legs scarcely able to support her.  Kabita Mu...
fullText:
GAUR, Nepal (AP) — The young mother's breath had grown ragged. Inside her mud home in rural Nepal, she hunched over in agony, pain pummeling her pregnant belly, her swollen legs scarcely able to support her.

Kabita Mukhiya was in the midst of an emergency, but didn't know it. For weeks, she'd suffered at home, because there was nobody around to tell her to rush to a hospital. The aid workers who once regularly visited her village to help pregnant women had stopped coming, after foreign aid cuts by the United States shuttered a program aimed at saving mothers' and babies' lives.

Kabita was uneducated and impoverished, and she did not know what was happening to her body. In desperation, she turned at last to her aunt for help, who hauled her off to the hospital, where both women wept as the doctors said things neither could understand.

Which is why Kabita — confused and confined to her hospital bed — turned to something she could understand: prayer.

"Please save the baby," she begged God through her tears. "Please save me."

Then, through the chaos, came the words that Kabita finally grasped, but could not bear: It was too late. Her baby was dead.

And her own life was now hanging by a thread.

This story was funded by a grant from the Pulitzer Center. The Associated Press is responsible for all content.

One baby at a time, the world is marching toward a grim milestone: Because of global cuts to foreign aid, the Gates Foundation has predicted that 2025 will be the first year this century where child deaths will increase.

For many experts, the health of a country is measured by the health of its smallest: Children under the age of 5. And while global child mortality data for 2025 won't be available for several months, health officials are already bracing for a surge in deaths among the world's youngest and most vulnerable.

The decision by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to dissolve the United States Agency for International Development — once the world's largest humanitarian donor — gutted maternal and neonatal care, decimated nutrition programs for millions of pregnant women and children and left scores of birthing centers devoid of equipment, medicine and staff. The U.S. cuts, followed by foreign aid cuts from several other countries, forced 60% of women's organizations to reduce their services, according to the World Health Organization.

The U.S. government has repeatedly insisted that no one — and, particularly, no children — have died because of its funding cuts. But the AP has documented the deaths of women and children from Myanmar to Nigeria.

A study published in The Lancet journal, meanwhile, said the U.S. cuts could lead to more than 14 million deaths, including more than 4.5 million children under age 5, by 2030.

"It's heartbreaking to see what's happening. It's decades of progress being washed away," says Rajat Khosla, executive director of WHO's Partnership for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health.

In a statement to The Associated Press, the U.S. State Department said the Trump administration had reinvigorated its assistance programs to focus on efficiency, effectiveness and partnership. The department also said the U.S. spends more on health and humanitarian assistance than any other country, and still supports programs in Nepal aimed at improving maternal and child health.

"The rest of the world needs to contribute more and share the burden," the department said.

In Nepal, cuts to nutrition and reproductive outreach programs have already increased pregnancy complications and deaths, according to health workers, government officials, aid workers and families interviewed by the AP.

"The number of deaths of mothers, young mothers, during delivery has really increased," says Mona Sherpa, country director for the aid group CARE Nepal, which lost more than half its funding from the U.S. cuts. "The expected number within a year is happening within four to six months."

Maternal and child health programs are perhaps the clearest foreign aid example of small, relatively cheap interventions leading to the greatest good. Packets of fortified peanut paste that cost less than a dollar each can bring a malnourished child back from the brink of death within weeks. Clean birth kits that cost a few dollars slash the risk of mothers and newborns dying from infections.

In Nepal, a five-year, $35 million program canceled by the U.S. cuts reached more than 100,000 women and girls in its first three years. The program equipped birthing centers and trained nurses, midwives and outreach workers known as female community health volunteers. These workers regularly visited pregnant women's homes, explained the warning signs of complications and urged them to attend prenatal appointments, often escorting them there.

When the program was canceled, many pregnant women were left to navigate a medical system they struggle to trust or understand, Sherpa says.

The consequences can be found in the dusty, sun-scorched villages of Nepal's Rautahat district, home to Kabita's family and one of the poorest and least-literate parts of the country. At a birthing center in Rautahat's municipality of Dewahi Gonahi, the number of women coming for prenatal checks has halved since the funding cuts, says the officer in charge, Kishori Shah. Because of that, women aren't identifying complications fast enough, he says, leading to emergencies.

"There would have been a decrease in complications if the USAID program was still running," he says.

In the village of Prempur Gonahi, it took just 10 months — a touch longer than a typical pregnancy — for newborns to begin dying again after the U.S. cuts, says the officer in charge, Sadho Baitha.

Before CARE's program launched in Rautahat in December 2022, Baitha says, the village averaged 10 to 15 neonatal deaths per year. By 2024, records show, there were zero. But since the program's cancellation, newborns have begun dying again; the first was in December, and four more followed by March.

Yet many deaths linked to the funding cuts will remain invisible, in part because the cuts themselves left scores of mortality data collectors jobless. In some places, there is simply no one left to count those who died.

This is the case in Dewahi Gonahi, where mortality reporting and recording services have collapsed, says Shatrudhan Singh, executive director of Campaign Nepal, CARE's partner. Which is why, he says, the government record shows just two infant deaths in the municipality since the funding cuts, despite his group knowing of eight.

"There must be more than that," he says. "We just can't identify them."

The stories of loss are hidden inside the cramped homes of the loved ones left behind and in the vacant eyes of now-motherless children.

From the shadows of her own home, Phula Devi tries to verbalize her loss in a voice so halting and hushed it's barely audible. She has never spoken of her grief to anyone — not even to her husband.

Like most women in this village a few miles from Kabita's, Phula never attended school. She knew almost nothing about pregnancy; she does not even know her own age, just that she is not yet 20.

Phula is the type of woman outreach workers say they would have targeted. Instead, one morning in January, an informal village health practitioner came to her home and said the fetal heartbeat was slow. He told her to go to a hospital, then left.

Phula didn't understand. And she was at the mercy of her relatives, who waited until that night to take her to the hospital.

There, the doctors urged a C-section. But Phula didn't know what that meant. Terrified, she pushed the baby out on her own. He emerged silent and still, declared dead and whisked away before Phula could hold him, name him or even see his face.

He was overdue, hospital records show, a risk factor for stillbirth. Nurse Guddi Rahami, who remembers Phula's case, says the region's uneducated families often resist C-sections because they believe the operation is somehow bad.

From inside her darkened home, Phula hides her tear-streaked face behind a scarf.

"I think of my baby all the time," she murmurs.

She would have done anything to save him, she says. If she'd only known how.

Down a winding dirt path peppered with bleating goats, Kabita's two-room home emerges into view. Outside, women trudge past in a rainbow of saris that cling to their fragile frames, seared by the punishing sun.

This became Kabita's home at 14, when she married her husband after a life of loss. Her mother died when she was little, and her father soon abandoned her to move to India with his new wife. Her three siblings would later follow him.

Her wedding photo shows her as the child she still was when she married: slender, with wide-set brown eyes, soft cheeks and a shy smile. She struggled to bond with her mother-in-law, who shared their home, but endeared herself to her aunt and neighbor, Shraddha Mukhiya. Shraddha relished Kabita's innocence and was amused by her constant, occasionally nonsensical, chatter. She came to view the girl as her daughter.

Kabita quickly fell pregnant with a daughter of her own, Sonam. Her second daughter, Anushka, followed a year later, and her son, Yubraj, a year after that.

Her husband, the family's sole provider, was rarely home, forced to chase construction jobs around Nepal and India that brought the family around 12,000 Nepalese rupees ($80) per month. It was enough to buy rice, lentils and vegetables, but little else.

Despite the difficulties, the 20-year-old Kabita was overjoyed to learn she was pregnant with her fourth; she and her mother-in-law longed for another boy. She scraped together enough money to buy clothes for the baby, whom she planned to name Shivraj, and dreamed that he would one day get the education she was never afforded.

When she was pregnant with Yubraj, she received a U.S.-funded nutritious powder that helped supplement her limited diet. But by the time she became pregnant last year, the funding cuts had eliminated the local birthing center's nutritional supplements and food for pregnant women, says Punam Mahato, a nurse who treated Kabita.

U.S.-funded nutrition programs were crucial to the region, particularly for children, health workers say. The prevalence of wasting — a life-threatening form of malnutrition — among children under 5 in Kabita's province was 7.4% before the U.S. funding cuts, according to a survey conducted by the government and the United Nations' children's agency. That number rose to 12.3% after the cuts, according to a national malnutrition screening conducted in May by the government and the aid group Helen Keller Intl, which saw its nutrition program halted by the U.S. cuts.

As her pregnancy progressed, Kabita's belly swelled while the rest of her remained gaunt. Sometimes she only managed to eat two small meals a day. And the mothers' group meetings she attended while pregnant with Yubraj had ceased.

She missed the recommended first trimester appointment, and made her first visit to the birthing center for a check at 16 weeks. Mahato, her nurse, noticed she was pale. She suggested Kabita get a blood test to check her hemoglobin, which can plummet in pregnancy amid nutritional deficiencies.

But Kabita never got the test, and didn't seem to understand its necessity; she never mentioned it to her mother-in-law. At 24 weeks, Mahato was worried by Kabita's pallid complexion and again recommended a blood test. Again, Kabita demurred, likely because she didn't grasp its importance, Mahato says.

Rajkumari Patel, a community health volunteer who worked under CARE's now-canceled program, said they would have acted as mediators to explain to Kabita why the test was crucial.

Instead, Kabita returned home. She was tormented by stomach pains that grew increasingly fierce. Her body swelled.

She suffered for weeks. By December, when she was 28 weeks pregnant, Kabita had become so weak she could not walk. Her husband was working in India, so she turned to Shraddha, her aunt, for help. The elder woman took her to the hospital.

Doctors drew Kabita's blood to check her hemoglobin levels, then handed the results to the women. But Kabita and Shraddha didn't know what they meant. Nor did they understand the rush of activity and tests and medical explanations that followed.

Their understanding finally came amid the absence of a heartbeat. A test confirmed it: Kabita's baby was dead.

Everything was happening so fast.

The hospital was not equipped to remove the baby's remains from Kabita's womb. Staffers urged them to go to another hospital. But with no money and no sense for the danger Kabita was facing, the grieving women returned home.

In desperation, Shraddha took her to another hospital with lower fees. The doctors determined that she'd had a seizure from preeclampsia, where dangerously high blood pressure can be fatal if untreated, says paramedic Hridaya Narayan Mahato, who is not related to Kabita's nurse.

Doctors gave her oxygen while the staff rushed to prepare the ICU.

Kabita's hemoglobin levels were critically low, leaving her short of oxygen and straining her heart. She lay on her back, shaking and gasping for air. Shraddha sat helplessly at the foot of the bed. "You'll be OK," she told her niece through tears.

And then she watched as Kabita drew her final breath.

She was dead before they could get her into the ICU.

A short drive from Kabita's home, Patel, the community health worker, sits outside her home, her words laced with frustration. Deaths like Kabita's, she says, are precisely what she and her colleagues had been trained to prevent.

Patel used to know every pregnant woman in her village, visiting them at home. She would have done the same for Kabita, she says.

"I would have asked her, 'Is the baby kicking? When did you last feel movement?' I would have checked for swelling in her hands and face. I would have looked at her eyes for signs of anemia," she says. "These are the signs I would have noticed in Kabita and said, 'This woman needs a hospital today -- not tomorrow.' Maybe we could have saved her life."

Kabita died from complications of eclampsia, with severe anemia contributing significantly, says Mahato, the hospital paramedic. Both conditions can often be identified and managed through regular prenatal care, he says.

The loss of Kabita and her baby so overwhelmed Shraddha that she couldn't bear to tell Kabita's husband. Still working in India, he was oblivious to the crisis until neighbors called him. His bus ride home took so long that he didn't arrive back in the village until three days after Kabita's funeral.

In the months since, he has frequently refused to work, lying in the dark crying for days at a time. He speaks only of Kabita, never the baby. Shraddha and his mother, Lachhiya Devi, remind him that they will all starve unless he returns to work. And so he does.

Both in their 60s, Shraddha and Lachhiya worry about how long they can care for Kabita's little ones. From the bed she shares with her grandchildren, Lachhiya strokes the leg of 4-year-old Anushka, who slumbers next to her in the midday heat.

"How will I feed them? I'm old," Lachhiya says, her bangles barely clinging to her bony arms. "You can see how desperately I'm trying to get by."

Their home is quiet now without Kabita's cheerful chatter or the cries of the baby who never made it home. The last reminders of Kabita's life — her sparkly green sari, the pink and yellow tapestry she knitted — are packed away in a box that will be given to her children one day.

Shraddha remains tormented by what she didn't know.

"We don't have anyone to help us out here, to tell us about these things. If there was someone, we would ask them, follow their advice," she says. "It would have saved her life."

She looks at Kabita's children and aches for their mother, who was barely beyond childhood herself.

Journalist Tulsi Rauniyar contributed to this report.

title: Russia is turning Kherson into a 'human safari' as its drones hunt civilians. Residents say anyone can be hit at any time.
description: Russia's drone attacks on civilians in Kherson have surged, turning daily life into a deadly "human safari."
fullText:
Russian drones target civilians in Kherson, escalating violence in the region.

In July, 26 people were killed by Russian drones. Hundreds more were injured.

Kherson residents say they live in fear as the city is under constant drone threat from Russian forces.

The shaky video that has horrified viewers around the world lasts just over 30 seconds.

It shows an exploding drone — small enough to fit in the palm of the hand and loaded with explosives — circling just meters above a vegetable seller's market stall in an area near the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson.

The distinctive buzzing of the aircraft is audible throughout the short video. Costing maybe only a few hundred euros, one-way attack drones like this are controlled by pilots using onboard cameras that provide a first-person view.

The Ukrainian vendor immediately recognizes the danger. He takes cover behind a white van parked beside his stall, constantly looking up at the threat above.

Like a predator stalking its prey, the drone circles, chasing him around the vehicle before suddenly diving toward him. It explodes as it hits the ground beside the van.

Today, many were shocked by yet another video of the drone "safari" Russians are carrying out against civilians in Kherson. A Russian drone deliberately hunted down a man selling vegetables and detonated right next to him. The Russians even admitted to the crime, showing zero… pic.twitter.com/uGjC7esFwR

— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) August 4, 2026

The vendor miraculously survived the August 4 attack, though he suffered multiple shrapnel wounds to his arms, legs, and back, as well as a concussion.

The name of the man in the video is Yuriy. He is 52 years old and lives in neighboring Mykolaiv. He regularly travels to Kherson with his wife to sell vegetables.

"The drone came from somewhere behind the market, from those bushes over there, and it was flying very low," Yuriy said in a video interview from the hospital that was released by Ukrainian authorities. "It is an open area. There is nowhere to go. It is frightening. Really frightening,"

"The Russians have gone mad," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, describing attacks of this kind by Russian forces as deliberate strikes against civilians in Kherson.

What makes the attack on Yuriy unusual is not necessarily the attack itself, but the fact that it was captured in such detail on video.

WELT's reporting in Kherson since late 2024 — including from some of the worst-affected riverside districts such as Richport — has documented how Russian drone pilots regularly hunt people in the southern Ukrainian city, both soldiers and civilians alike.

Cars, ambulances, and pedestrians are targeted. Anyone can be hit at any time, residents say.

In Ukraine, these attacks have become known as Russia's "human safari."

"The Russians mostly attack cars and buses. There have also been many attacks on medical personnel and ambulances," Alexander Tolokonnikov, a spokesman for Kherson's military administration, told WELT.

Using his mobile phone, Tolokonnikov documents the different types of Russian attacks across the city. Since autumn 2024, explosive devices dropped or carried by drones have rained down with increasing frequency.

In recent months, Russian forces have dramatically intensified their drone attacks on civilians in the Kherson region. Residents have described the escalation, and official statistics provided by Tolokonnikov point to the same trend.

In January, four people were killed and 28 were wounded. In February, two were killed and 53 were wounded. March saw seven killed and 66 wounded; April, 12 killed and 147 wounded; May, 11 killed and 201 wounded; and June, 10 killed and 179 wounded.

Then came a dramatic surge in July: 26 people killed and 421 wounded by Russian drone attacks in a single month.

While WELT was unable to independently verify every individual case reported, the broader trend is unmistakable.

"This is clearly a war crime when they fly an explosive-laden drone directly into civilians or into an ambulance," Col. Markus Reisner, an Austrian military officer, told WELT.

Reisner has analyzed numerous videos of the drone attacks and believes there is a clear strategic calculation behind them.

"The Russians are trying in Kherson to drive the population away from the other side of the river and make this area uninhabitable," he said.

It is depopulation carried out with lethal precision.

The drone hunt against civilians has become part of Russia's approach to Kherson since Moscow lost control of the city.

In the first days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin's troops seized central Kherson. The occupation lasted eight months.

During a Ukrainian counteroffensive, Russian forces were forced to retreat across the Dnipro River, and Ukraine liberated the city in November 2022.

Since then, Ukrainian and Russian forces have faced each other across the Dnipro, separated in places by only a few kilometers. The city is under fire day and night.

Over the past few years, WELT has confirmed multiple drone attacks on civilians in Kherson and spoken with the victims and local authorities.

Video footage of these hunts is sometimes openly displayed on pro-Russian Telegram channels.

The British non-profit Centre for Information Resilience (CIR) had already verified several such videos by the end of 2024. Its investigation found a "clear escalation" in drone attacks by Russian forces.

Olga Chernyshova survived one such attack in Kherson in September 2024.

A drone targeted her as she returned from shopping and parked her car.

"The drone was flying very low and making that noise. I immediately ran toward the house, and then it exploded behind me," Chernyshova said.

Her vehicle was badly damaged, but she escaped physically unharmed. In 2025, Chernyshova was running the last remaining shop in Richport, her heavily bombed neighborhood.

Volodymyr Shemenkov manages the last brewery on the outskirts of Kherson. Russian missiles have already struck its premises, as CCTV footage shows.

He said he personally knows numerous civilians who have been attacked by Russian exploding drones.

At the end of 2024, one of his workers was hit by a Russian drone attack as he stepped out of a taxi. "He was hit by a grenade dropped from a drone. It landed right next to his leg," Shemenkov told WELT last year.

His employee was taken to the hospital with serious injuries.

"If I tell you I'm not afraid, that would not be true. The truth is that every one of us is afraid. Nobody is safe anymore. When you walk down the street, you have to expect every second that a drone could hit you," Shemenkov said.

Before Russia's full-scale invasion, more than a quarter of a million people lived in Kherson. Most have fled; others are fighting at the front. Only around 50,000 to 60,000 residents remain.

Increasingly, everyday life is moving underground.

"Many of the people who are still here are fatalists," Aleksandra Kniga, who works with children and teenagers in Kherson, told WELT. "It is our fate whether we are killed in our homes or not. That is why we do not want to leave."

On April 2, Kniga experienced for herself just how omnipresent the threat of Russian drones has become.

She was walking through Kherson's Shumensky district looking for a new shelter for the children because the place they had previously been using had become too dangerous.

Previously, the neighborhood had been considered relatively safe.

"In April," Kniga said, "it became absolute hell." Drone attacks had increased dramatically.

As she walked through the streets, she said she heard shotgun fire getting closer and closer — apparent attempts to shoot a drone out of the sky.

Shortly afterward, her drone detector sounded an alarm. Devices like these are now carried by civilians as well as soldiers.

Kniga started running but could find almost no cover.

She just managed to reach the covered entrance of an apartment building when a drone came down nearby and exploded.

The blast left her with explosion-related trauma and a concussion. That the drone did not fragment into a large number of pieces probably saved her from more serious injuries, she said.

Every day, Kniga says, people in Kherson are wounded or killed by Russian exploding drones. Most attacks, however, are never captured on video.

At the same time, Russian propaganda repeatedly attempts to blame such attacks on Ukraine, or even claims that Ukrainians are killing their own civilians.

"This is the reality we live with," Kniga said. "This is how Russia terrorizes the people of Kherson every single day."

Ibrahim Naber is a foreign correspondent who has reported from Ukraine since 2022. In October 2025, he and his team were injured in a Russian Lancet drone strike in Dnipro. In 2025, he received the George Weidenfeld Prize for his coverage of global conflicts and crisis zones. He wrote his dissertation at King's College London on the psychology of modern drone warfare.

This story, which first ran on WELT, comes courtesy of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces, and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from The Telegraph, POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Fighter jets intercept plane over Ohio, where Trump attended event
description: Last month, fighter jets also intercepted planes attempting to fly near MetLife Stadium, during the World Cup Final.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Fighter jets intercepted a plane that entered restricted airspace Tuesday over Geneva, Ohio, where President Donald Trump was attending an event, military officials said.

F-16 fighter jets used flares to alert the pilot after the plane violated a temporary flight restriction, according to the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD).

The interception occurred Tuesday around 6:15 p.m. ET. The civilian aircraft was safely escorted out of the restricted airspace.

NORAD said the flares are designed with safety in mind, "burn out quickly and completely, and pose no danger to people on the ground." Officials noted they may have been visible from the ground.

The temporary flight restriction was issued by the Federal Aviation Administration as Trump traveled to Ohio to attend the 2026 Patriot Games, a youth athletic tournament backed by the White House.

The incident comes days after NORAD fighter jets intercepted planes over Bedminster, New Jersey, where Trump owns a golf course. Two general aviation aircraft violated temporary flight restrictions Sunday and were safely escorted out of the restricted airspace.

Officials said the restrictions are intended to protect airspace around sensitive locations and major events.

Last month, fighter jets intercepted multiple planes attempting to fly in temporarily restricted airspace over Bedminster and East Rutherford, N.J. NORAD said flares were deployed to get the attention of two pilots.

The interceptions occurred while international leaders and celebrities gathered in East Rutherford for the World Cup Final at MetLife Stadium.

The FAA issues temporary flight restrictions for a variety of reasons, including major events involving high-profile political figures. Pilots are notified of the restrictions through Notices to Airmen, or NOTAMs, and NORAD and the FAA urged pilots to check those notices before flying.

title: That Chrome Update Pop-Up May Actually Be Malware
description: Malicious extensions are to blame.
fullText:
If you're seeing pop-ups in Chrome pushing you to download an update in order to continue browsing or avoid losing access to your data, you may be a target for malware. As Android Authority reports, compromised browser extensions appear to be distributing malicious scripts disguised as "critical" security updates.

Some Google Chrome users have noticed aggressive pop-ups alerting them to required updates and prompting them to download the latest version of the browser. One version states that "access to websites is temporarily blocked" until the update is installed. The other is even more urgent, stating that Chrome will stop working after a certain date and require a "complete reinstallation," in which users may lose access to bookmarks, history, and saved passwords. If you click "Update Chrome," it'll download a suspicious .vbs or .exe script to your device.

The issue seems to be traceable to a handful of extensions, which are fetching malicious scripts and serving fake prompts inside the browser. In Chrome, one such add-on is “Enable Right Click & Copy Smart Unlock + OCR," which has a "Featured" tag and 70,000 downloads (though other utility tools may be culprits as well). Users on Brave and Opera, both Chromium browsers, have reported identical pop-ups. For the former, the compromised extension, called "QuickLens – Search Screen with Google Lens," was removed from the Web Store.

While some malicious add-ons do find their way onto the Chrome Web Store, it's not uncommon for threat actors to weaponize otherwise benign extensions after gaining platform approval and user trust. In campaigns identified across Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and Firefox, hackers have built extensions posing as crypto wallet and productivity apps, let them operate legitimately to rack up downloads and reviews, and then pushed updates that turned them into malware.

This is an effective strategy because malicious extensions can evade detection by antivirus software and system scans. The browser itself isn't compromised—rather, the add-on is pulling malicious scripts from a remote server, and the threat isn't picked up until you actually download and execute them on your device.

If you start seeing pop-ups for critical security updates in your browser, don't click on them, and don't copy or install anything from them. The alerts in this campaign have fairly convincing Chrome branding and elements like a copyright and links to a privacy policy and terms of service, but beware the sense of urgency. You can check whether your browser actually needs to be updated in the settings menu (on Chrome, click the three vertical dots or go to Settings > About Chrome).

You should also regularly check the extensions you've added to your browser and delete any that aren't essential. Click the extensions icon > Manage Extensions to see what's active and review permissions granted. If you're still getting sketchy pop-ups, try removing utility apps to see if you can identify the culprit.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Lanterns' You Should Watch Next
description: More shows that take superheroes to unconventional places. (Like Nebraska.)
fullText:
Under James Gunn's tenure, the DC Universe has promised us variety, and in that spirit, we're soon getting Lanterns, a show that stars Kyle Chandler as veteran Green Lantern Hal Jordan and Aaron Pierre as new recruit John Stewart fighting evil...in Nebraska. The two superheroes find themselves investigating a murder in a tiny town, a far cry from the typical intergalactic adventures of the Green Lantern Corps, space cops who can create just about anything with their fancy-schmancy rings. (Though it's not without precedent, as the 1970s comics saw Hal team up with Green Arrow to travel the country and see how we live here on the ground.)

It's obviously early days for the new HBO Max series, and it is as yet unclear whether it will be viewed as a clever genre twist or a too-constrained waste of potential. Either way, Lanterns won't be the first show to push the boundaries of the sci-fi and superhero genres. Here are 10 others that have arguably pulled it off.

A standalone sequel to the groundbreaking Alan Moore, Dave Gibbons, and John Higgins graphic novel from the '80s, this series plays in the sandbox of that book (arguably the wellspring of all modern superhero deconstruction), with a little help from Lanterns co-creator Damon Lindelof. In an alternate Tulsa, Oklahoma, in a world where super-powered vigilantes exist and have been outlawed, the series starts with a depiction of the real-life massacre and destruction of Tulsa's Black Wall Street by white residents in 1921. Regina King plays Angela Abar, a modern cop whose grandparents were killed during those attacks, events that echo throughout the series, which focuses on the fallout from the plot of the original comic and the conspiracies that grew out of it. Like Lanterns, this show's focus is on life on the ground in a world where gods fly above. Stream Watchmen on HBO Max or buy episodes from Prime Video.

Almost certainly the best adaptation of Green Lantern to date, this show, from some of the people behind Batman: The Animated Series, doesn't take a grounded approach in the least, instead going in quite the opposite direction. Instead, it mines decades of comics' lore to send GL and company into deep space for some of the biggest adventures imaginable. Hal Jordan (Josh Keaton) is one of the finest Lanterns in the Corps, but his reputation for recklessness has led his superiors to distrust him. When he learns that rage-fueled Red Lanterns are murdering his compatriots in deep space, he defies orders and steals a prototype ship to help. Things get complicated on the frontier, as the show balances individual adventures with a longer storyline about the nature of the Red Lanterns, and whether their green counterparts are entirely the good guys. Buy Green Lantern: The Animated Series from Prime Video.

There's nothing new about going grim-and-gritty with stories set in Gotham City, so this is perhaps slightly less of a departure than Lanterns—still, a prestige crime drama in a superhero world was new-ish territory way back in 2024. A spin-off of the latest Batman movie (the Robert Pattinson one), the show stars Colin Farrell as the up-and-coming mobster of the title. In the wake of the killing of boss Carmine Falcone. the Penguin and the absolutely unhinged Sofia Falcone (Cristin Milioti, who won an Emmy for the role) are vying for control of the underworld. After decades of live-action Batman tales, it's kind of refreshing to see what's going on in Gotham City when the Caped Crusader has his back turned. Stream The Penguin on HBO Max.

It's saying quite a bit to suggest that Elizabeth Tulloch and Tyler Hoechlin are among the finest live-action Lois and Clark pairings ever, but here we are. Skipping over the will-they/won't-they of earlier takes, the show jumps ahead to find the two married and with two teenage children, Jonathan and Jordan. The couple has just moved back to Smallville to give the kids a semblance of a normal life. Good luck with that! The show balances small-town drama with big superhero stakes, never more so than in the later seasons, when community-minded crime boss Bruno Mannheim (Chad L. Coleman) uses a Bizarro-style clone to put Superman out of his way while their wives both battle cancer. Stream Superman & Lois on HBO Max.

Here's an uncharacteristically bold and indescribably freaky entry in the superhero canon, including characters like the non-binary Danny the Street (a literal street), paranormal investigators the Sex Men, Imaginary Jesus, and orgasm-generating bodybuilder Flex Mentallo. All the weirdness is grounded in excellent, frequently emotional character work from the entire cast, including Brendan Fraser, Matt Bomer, April Bowlby, Diane Guerrero, Joivan Wade, Michelle Gomez, and Timothy Dalton. It’s queer and sex-positive, making it a standout among the usually chaste, straight world of superheroes on TV. Stream Doom Patrol on HBO Max.

There's a lot of Batman out there, but this one's got real style, harkening back to Batman: The Animated Series from the 1990s (no surprise, given that Bruce Timm developed this one too). With a 1940s-esque setting, the show dodges some of the more outlandish superhero tropes to focus on a Gotham City rife with crime, corrupt cops, and gang warfare. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, exactly, but it's a strong enough reimagining that it feels fresh, particularly given that every other superhero show seems to require a deep investment in crossovers and spin-offs. Stream Batman: Caped Crusader Prime Video.

This animated show sees Amanda Waller (Viola Davis, reprising the role from the live-action DC movies) assembling a black-ops team to protect a foreign nation from the Amazonian sorceress Circe. Waller can't be trusted with actual humans, so her team is made up entirely of literal monsters: The Bride (Indira Varma), Doctor Phosphorus (Alan Tudyk), Eric Frankenstein (David Harbour), and aquatic mutant Nina Mazursky (Zoë Chao), alongside Nazi-obsessed G.I. Robot and the rodent-like Weasel (both Sean Gunn). Extremely violent and with a dark sense of humor, this show from James Gunn and company also brings an impressive amount of heart to the mix. Plus, it's set in the same relatively young universe as Lanterns, so you won't be behind on your homework. Stream Creature Commandos on HBO Max.

Alaqua Cox returns to her Hawkeye role of Maya Lopez, a deaf assassin who once worked for Vincent D'Onofrio's Wilson Fisk. She's now on the run from the mob boss, returning to her hometown in Oklahoma to come to terms with her past and to reconnect with her family and roots in the Choctaw Nation. The personal stakes mark a welcome shift toward the personal and away from the multiversal scale of the most recent Marvel—even as the show's scope encompasses centuries of Choctaw history. Stream Echo on Disney+.

They might be galaxies apart, but if you're looking for a grounded show born from a sci-fi premise, look no further than Andor. Just when I felt like I was done with Star Wars, along came this prequel series, the morally complex story of thief-turned-rebel spy Cassian Andor (Diego Luna) being radicalized and setting out on the road to becoming the heart and soul of the Rebellion. We witness the slow march of the Empire, as citizens of the galaxy become acclimated to rising fascism, and delve into the conflicts between various rebel factions: Genevieve O'Reilly's Mon Mothma fights from within the Galactic Senate, while Stellan Skarsgård's Luthen Rael, Andor's handler, favors dark deeds done under cover of darkness. Forest Whitaker's Saw Gerrera is content to burn the Galaxy down rather than allow it to become what he hates. The scope is grand, but the focus is very much on the people at the bottom of the ladder, and what they do or don't do in the face of tyranny. There's also a lot of dust. Stream Andor on Disney+.

There's been a lot of talk about Lanterns being the DC universe's explicit answer to True Detective, so here we are. This crime anthology started out by taking us to Oklahoma, with Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson investigating a murder that led to a broader mystery that bordered on the cosmic. The most recent season similarly sees veteran Chief Liz Danvers (Jodie Foster) and Trooper Evangeline Navarro (Kali Reis) face their complicated pasts while searching for missing scientists at a research station in a remote Alaskan town. Stream True Detective on HBO Max.

title: Apple TV Just Added These 'Classic' Movies to Its Catalog for Free
description: You can stream "E.T." and "Titanic" for free on Apple TV right now.
fullText:
Over the past seven years, Apple TV has slowly become the streaming service to beat. The platform now has a plethora of must-see TV programs, from buzzy hits like Ted Lasso, Severance, and Shrinking to strong sci-fi fare like Foundation and Silo—not to mention Apple Original movies, including Killers of the Flower Moon, F1, and Coda. While the streaming service isn't the first platform that comes to mind for non-Apple content, it does occasionally license shows and movies in addition to its own original programming—including, notably, those old Peanuts specials—and as of today, that licensed catalog just got a bit bigger.

As spotted by 9to5Mac, Apple TV has added 19 movies to its catalog that subscribers can watch for free, without paying a separate rental fee. The selection runs the gamut, featuring films from the 80s, 90s, 2000s, and 2010s and spanning genres and subject matter. Though not all of these movies are exactly awards material, a number of them are considered classics in their own right, from older hits like E.T. and Titanic to recently lauded movies like Arrival. Each of them is free to watch with any Apple TV subscription, and you can find them in the platform's "Great Movies Available Now on Apple TV" section.

Here is the complete list of all the movies Apple TV just added to its catalog for free:21 Jump Street

Mission Impossible: Ghost Protocol

It's unclear how long these movies will remain on Apple TV, or whether Apple plans to add more movies to the mix in the future. As 9to5Mac highlights, it's not the first time Apple has licensed movies in this way, though it has been several years, and previously, Apple has removed the offerings from the platform in short order. All of these movies are available to rent or buy through Apple's digital store too, so if you miss out on the window, you can always pay a rental fee to view them.

title: When they didn’t find fraud while testing a voting machine for the Trump admin, this cyber firm faced a wave of backlash
description: The Trump administration abruptly declined to renew a contract for a cybersecurity firm it hired to examine voting equipment in Puerto Rico after the company didn’t echo administration officials’ fals...
fullText:
The Trump administration abruptly declined to renew a contract for a cybersecurity firm it hired to examine voting equipment in Puerto Rico after the company didn't echo administration officials' false claims of voter fraud, the firm's executives said in their first extensive public remarks on the episode.

After hearing that the firm had found no evidence of vote tampering, allies of President Donald Trump derailed the cybersecurity firm's work with the government in part by spreading false claims that the firm was funded by liberal billionaire George Soros, according to the firm's executives and documents they provided to CNN.

A group of "White House-adjacent" Trump allies was "dissatisfied" that "I was not willing to name and shame at that moment and to say, 'Turns out 2020 was a landslide for Trump. Nobody knew,'" Jason Wareham, CEO of the firm Mojave Research, said this month at the DEF CON cybersecurity conference in Las Vegas.

Mojave Research had no prior experience in testing election systems when the Office of the Director of National Intelligence contacted them in the spring of 2025 as part of the agency's broader probe into voting equipment. ODNI hired the firm to analyze a specific voting machine made by Liberty Vote (formerly Dominion Voting Systems) that the agency acquired from Puerto Rico. Mojave did the work in six weeks in Wareham's basement in Reston, Virginia, according to Wareham.

Mojave submitted a report on their findings to ODNI in July 2025, Wareham said, but it has yet to be made public. However, Mojave chief technology officer Manbir Gulati described the findings in detail at DEF CON's "Voting Village" symposium.

"We found extensive and largely unacceptable weaknesses, but we did not find evidence that those weaknesses were actively exploited or that votes were altered," Gulati said.

What Wareham's team found — and didn't find — in his basement would become a Rorschach test for Trump administration officials focused on election issues. It's a cautionary tale of how a company that says it wanted to provide the administration with unbiased election security analysis was rejected by a group of officials who still dispute the results of the 2020 election and have Trump's ear. The Trump administration's revisiting of the 2020 election has extended to Arizona, where the FBI has obtained records of an audit that confirmed Joe Biden won the state.

After the company made clear what it had found, multiple figures aligned with Trump began to cast doubt on the integrity of Mojave, according to Wareham.

Wareham, a Republican, submitted a declaration in September under the penalty of perjury to the Trump administration to refute the notion that his company was "some form of deep plant meant to ensure the suppression of truth around compromised elections or election systems," the declaration says.

Wareham submitted his declaration and financial statements to ODNI to prove he was not affiliated with Soros, who has long been the subject of antisemitic conspiracy theories about secret levers of power. The next month, Wareham said he received an email, reviewed by CNN, which said that ODNI had issued a "stop-work order" on the contract.

The declaration alleges that Olsen repeatedly inserted himself into a probe of voting equipment begun last year by ODNI under a program known as the Director's Initiatives Group.

Olsen had no experience in election law prior to the 2020 election, but he gained traction in Trump's orbit — and eventually a direct line to the president — for trying to challenge elections in court. The Arizona Supreme Court ordered $2,000 in sanctions against Olsen and his co-counsel after they made false claims about the 2022 Arizona gubernatorial election in their failed effort to overturn that result.

"During many of those interactions and meetings, Mr. Olsen would inform me he was speaking with [t]he President on the election topic and at times seemed to intimate that he spoke on this issue for him," Wareham's declaration says. Olsen did not become a special government employee at the White House until October 2025, but Wareham told CNN that Olsen would routinely attend ODNI meetings on election security prior.

After Mojave's contract ended with ODNI, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard was present in Fulton County, Georgia, in January as the FBI seized records related to the 2020 election. Gabbard's presence, which she said Trump requested, alarmed election officials from both parties. Olsen drafted the criminal referral to the Justice Department that led to the FBI seizure.

Wareham's declaration spotlights Olsen's alleged actions in the months prior to the FBI seizure in Georgia. Discussions involving Olsen and others in his orbit were "hindered by rampant conjecture and assertions made without supporting evidence or documentation," the document says.

"I lost count the number of times I heard 'Maricopa County is a crime scene,'" Wareham said in his declaration. Maricopa County is Arizona's largest county and has been at the center of Trump allies' false claims that the 2020 election was stolen.

"In total, despite requests and invitations to provide us materials that could be fully integrated into our reporting, we have received little to nothing that would support anything that Mr. Olsen has said or that would allow us to do a primary forensic analysis of sufficient quality that the [Director of National Intelligence] could rely on our conclusions," the declaration says.

Olsen, now a Justice Department employee, did not respond to multiple requests for comment, nor did the ODNI. The Justice Department had no comment other than to say that Olsen did not join the department until June. The White House referred questions to the ODNI.

Liberty Vote said it would not comment on Mojave's findings because it had not seen the report Mojave submitted to ODNI, but added that it "is committed to advancing the future of secure American elections."

ODNI officials accepted Mojave's findings, according to Gulati and Wareham. The split within the administration over the Mojave report and the delay over releasing it has undercut efforts to fix the software flaws in the voting equipment, the Mojave executives said.

"What we encountered [were] a lot of competing factions within the government — people who want the boogey man to be out there and are willing to do anything to find it and then people who actually do genuinely care about the issue [of election security]," Gulati added. "There was a huge faction that was like, 'Mojave doesn't know what they're doing. They're dummies and that's why they can't find evidence of compromise."

Cybersecurity research of election systems has become a fraught exercise after the 2020 election because of the tendency of conspiracy theorists to equate software bugs with voter fraud.

Gulati said he wrestled with the decision to work with the administration, given the risk his research could be weaponized.

"Because their motivations were off, that doesn't necessarily mean that the idea of looking into election security is wrong or something that shouldn't be prioritized," Gulati said, adding that he would rather contribute his security expertise than stay silent. "There have been plenty of pushes for election security efforts both on the left and the right, as there should be."

title: Former Kohberger defense expert says he stalked Madison Mogen
description: Sy Ray says cellphone data points to Madison Mogen as the suspect's primary target.
fullText:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OWQuaZW62_4

(NewsNation) — One of the experts Bryan Kohberger's defense team hired before he pleaded guilty says cellphone data points to Madison Mogen as the suspect's primary target.

Sy Ray, a digital forensics expert, told NewsNation's Brian Entin he believes Kohberger stalked Mogen and was in the University of Idaho student's home before the killings.

Kohberger pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty in the 2022 murders of Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Madison Mogen, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20.

As Kohberger now attempts to withdraw his guilty plea and reopen the case, these revelations could come up in court.

Ray has access to cellphone data not publicly seen, and according to that data, Mogen and Kohberger were in the same place multiple times, Entin reported. That includes an A&W restaurant and an apartment next door to Kohberger's in Pullman, Washington, a nearby town to Moscow, Idaho.

Ray also believes Kohberger was stalking the house where Mogen, Goncalves and Kernodle lived.

The house is on a dead-end street on a hill — the "strangest location for a house," Entin reported. "There's no way you would just drive by the house. It makes zero sense."

title: Cardiff aim to prove doubters wrong - Barry-Murphy
description: Boss Brian Barry-Murphy says Cardiff City aim to disprove pundits who have dismissed them as possible relegation candidates in 2026-27
fullText:
Head coach Brian Barry-Murphy says Cardiff City will try to prove the doubters wrong after some pundits tipped them to struggle on their return to the Championship.

Barry-Murphy says Cardiff feel they can "surprise some people" in the second tier after finishing runners-up in League One in 2025-26.

The 48-year-old would not be drawn on where he thinks the Bluebirds can finish in the Championship, but suggested bookmakers and pundits are wrong to write them off as possible relegation candidates.

"We saw a lot of predictions this week which put us in the bottom two or bottom three - it's not a problem for us to have predictions like that, but we'll be looking to prove them wrong," Barry-Murphy told BBC Sport Wales.

"We're under no illusions about how difficult the season is going to be - we're not naive, we're aware of the powerhouse teams we're going to face.

"But the size of the challenge improves the size of our excitement. The bigger the challenge, the more we look forward to it."

Fighting relegation & eyeing promotion? Championship set for six-team play-offs

Latest Cardiff City news, analysis and fan views

Asked what would constitute a successful season for his side, Barry-Murphy said: "We don't know. I think one of the beauties of this season is that, for a lot of us, we're going into the unknown.

"Our feeling is that we can surprise a lot of people. We have a real hunger and appetite to improve on what we did last season."

Barry-Murphy is preparing for a blockbuster start to the campaign, with Welsh rivals Wrexham at the Cardiff City Stadium for a south-north derby on 17 August.

The former Manchester City academy coach says he is unsure whether any more new signings will be completed ahead of Wrexham's visit, with Lincoln City midfielder Jack Moylan still the only outfield player recruited by Cardiff this summer.

"I don't think so," said Barry-Murphy when asked if Cardiff were close to a new signing.

"If you start anticipating timings or what may or may not happen, you just waste a lot of your time and your energy.

"Our focus is purely on the game on Monday and making sure that anything that could or maybe would distract us, doesn't."

Barry-Murphy said injured Wales forward Rubin Colwill could return for Wrexham's visit, but fellow international Dylan Lawlor is unlikely to be fit to face the Red Dragons.

title: West Ham's boardroom battle on eve of Championship season
description: As West Ham get ready to start their first league campaign outside the top flight since 2011-12, what's going on in the boardroom?
fullText:
West Ham head into their first Championship campaign for 14 years with fresh hope on the pitch but there remain significant questions off it, as a complex battle for control of the club continues.

Hammers fans have had plenty of good news this summer - manager Nuno Espirito Santo committed his future to the club along with captain Jarrod Bowen, while new arrivals Manor Solomon and Joel Veltman have added experience to the squad.

They have lost Mateus Fernandes to Tottenham and Crysencio Summerville to Saudi Pro League club Al Hilal, but supporters have reacted positively despite relegation, with 50,000 season tickets sold.

Yet uncertainty continues to swirl around the club's future ownership, two months after David Sullivan resigned from his position as co-chair after seven women accused him of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour - allegations he categorically denies.

Fellow co-chairs Vanessa Gold and Daniel Kretinsky vowed to protect the club, which appeared to be a straightforward agreement that would increase Czech billionaire Kretinsky's stake and make him the club's dominant shareholder.

It has since turned into a complicated corporate struggle after Gold's decision to sell her shares to a consortium led by former Newcastle United co-owner Amanda Staveley.

Kretinsky's subsequent move - selling 2% of his share to countryman Jakub Havrlant - raised fresh questions about how any takeover can be completed within the club's existing shareholder agreements.

Will West Ham bounce straight back up?

How will relegated trio fare in the Championship?

On 13 June - a week after West Ham co-chair and director Sullivan stood down to fight what he described as "false allegations" against him following a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times - Gold and Kretinsky released a joint statement.

"We were deeply concerned by the revelations, and our thoughts go out to those women who have fought so hard to make their voices heard," it said. "Any abuse of power is abhorrent, and it takes great courage and determination to speak up against it.

"Our focus is now firmly on protecting the future of this football club."

Despite his resignation, Sullivan remains the club's largest shareholder with 38.8%. He ignored the advice of London Stadium officials and requests from fan groups to stay away from their EFL Cup match against Portsmouth.

They won that match 3-1 in front of a crowd of 53,369 that smashed the record for the first round of the competition by over 18,000.

But the statement of reassurance from Gold and Kretinsky seems a long time ago as the Hammers prepare to begin their league season with a trip to Burnley.

Sullivan has been the subject of long-standing criticism from West Ham fans for his running of the club.

Together with former business partner and co-chair David Gold, who died in 2023, and Baroness Karren Brady, Sullivan has never been forgiven by some supporters for the decision to leave Upton Park in 2016 and move into the former Olympic Stadium.

Brady stood down as vice-chair on 21 April to focus on her other business interests.

In their June statement, Kretinsky, who owns 27%, and Gold (25.1%) said they had reached an agreement that meant the former, who also owns the Royal Mail, would become West Ham's biggest shareholder, with 43%.

The club's other significant shareholders - Tripp Smith, Daniel Harris and Terry Brown - were said to be in support.

But the deal was never completed.

On 1 August, Gold, who had initially put her shares up for sale in October 2023, confirmed "the original deal and other alternatives could not be brought to fruition" and announced she had agreed to sell her entire shareholding to a consortium headed by Staveley.

Kretinsky reacted with dismay, and said he was "considering his options". Three days later, it was confirmed Havrlant had bought just over 2% of his shares.

The backdrop to Kretinsky's move is West Ham's complicated pre-emption rights, and also a second agreement around share purchases.

Put simply, any major shareholder at West Ham who comes to an agreement to sell their shares has to first offer them to existing shareholders for the same amount on a pro-rata basis. The offer has to be open for 30 days.

In theory, Sullivan could buy just over half of Gold's shares - 13%. It would take him over 50% and Kretinsky could add an additional 9%.

Any sale would be scrutinised by the Independent Regulator, the introduction of which Sullivan and Brady were fiercely opposed to.

Sources close to Kretinsky think the regulator would step in to prevent Sullivan increasing his stake given the allegations against him, but that theory is yet to be tested.

Regardless, there is another key element of West Ham's share structure that forces anyone who takes their stake above 50% to offer to buy the remainder at a significantly inflated price.

It is that rule Kretinsky would circumvent through his deal with Havrlant as, if he ends up buying Gold's 25.1% of the club, he would still be under the 50% threshold.

However, this is also complicated.

For a start, Kretinsky's share sale is subject to the same pre-emption rights deal as Gold's.

Then, there is debate over whether it would be regarded, legally, as an attempt to get round a contractual obligation.

If all that wasn't enough, there have been suggestions Staveley's consortium has also made an offer for Sullivan's stake, although this has not been confirmed.

There are various theories over what is going on and why but, as yet, none of Sullivan, Gold, Kretinsky or Staveley have outlined their wider strategy in public.

It is complicated, and has left many supporters confused about which side they should be on.

"We had a real opportunity this summer to draw a line under what's been a pretty miserable period, get everyone pulling in the same direction and have a proper go at the season," said one long-standing supporter, with detailed knowledge of the club.

"Instead, we've got another West Ham soap opera playing out in the boardroom. It's like Eastenders."

title: When do the major European leagues start and what are the big stories?
description: BBC Sport looks at the big stories in Europe heading into the 2026-27 season.
fullText:
The start of the Premier League may still be a week off, but in Europe the new season is already getting under way.

With La Liga kicking off this weekend and Ligue 1, Serie A and the Bundesliga soon to follow, there are plenty of storylines to look forward to this season.

BBC Sport rounds up the best and looks ahead to what should be an enthralling campaign on the continent.

First La Liga match: Alaves v Getafe, Saturday 15 August, 18:30 (BST)

Jose Mourinho returning to Real Madrid 13 years after his first spell as manager ended was a reunion nobody saw coming.

Many expected Real to dominate La Liga and the Champions League when they signed Kylian Mbappe in 2024, and while he has impressed, the team as a whole has not gelled.

Last season Real looked like two teams on the same pitch - a group of four superstar attackers, and a fragile defensive unit left vulnerable to counter-attacks.

New signings Marc Cucurella, Ibrahima Konate, Denzel Dumfries and Bernardo Silva should help shore things up, while Yan Diomande could provide even more excitement in the final third.

Vinicius Junior has also recently agreed a new deal after being linked with Arsenal.

Some suggest a veteran Mourinho has had his day - can he manage the egos of Mbappe, Jude Bellingham and Vinicius after his previous time in charge at the Bernabeu ended following dressing room disquiet, and does the Special One still possess the tactical acumen to seriously challenge Barcelona?

Hansi Flick's side were not as formidable last season as in 2024-25, but a squad full of Spanish World Cup winners are still favourites to win a third consecutive league title.

Replacing the goals of Robert Lewandowski will not be easy, but reinforcements have arrived in the shape of Anthony Gordon and Karim Adeyemi.

As usual, Atletico Madrid will look to muscle their way into the top two, with Villarreal and Real Betis heading up the best of the rest.

After fighting their way up from the third tier, Malaga will look to avoid the drop with a budget but tightknit squad - they have been under judicial administration since 2020.

There will be tears in Valencia as Los Che play their final campaign at the iconic Mestalla stadium, but who knows if Uefa Conference League runners-up Rayo Vallecano will be able to play any home games at all.

The regional government of Madrid has stripped the club of its license to host matches at its rented Vallecas stadium due to the dilapidated state of the facilities.

La Liga to inspect Celta Vigo's pitch after fungus outbreak

New season, new boss - will Alexander-Arnold be key figure at Real Madrid?

First Serie A matches: Udinese v Como & Inter Milan v Monza, Saturday 22 August, 17:30 (BST)

Inter Milan are fancied to defend their Serie A crown, albeit partly because few teams look equipped to challenge them.

Napoli, AC Milan, Atalanta and Lazio all have new managers, while Juventus and Milan are both under pressure after missing out on the top four last term.

While the absence of Champions League football could aid their title bids, playing Thursday nights in the Europa League could hinder them.

How Ruben Amorim gets on at San Siro will be particularly interesting for Manchester United fans.

Napoli, whose two most recent title defences have fallen disappointingly flat, will hope Max Allegri can rediscover his knack for winning.

Como were the big story of last season, but can Cesc Fabregas' side replicate their league success while navigating a debut Champions League campaign?

They face a race against time to complete improvements at their idyllic lakeside stadium if they are to host European games.

Given the recent struggles of the Italian national team, Fabregas has pledged to try and bring through more young Italian players. Will others follow suit?

Roma did well to finish third last season after a rocky start, and have backed manager Gian Piero Gasperini in the transfer market. Can they kick on and win a first Scudetto since 2001?

Mourners line streets of Milan for legend Baresi's funeral

Defender Stones joins Inter Milan on free transfer

First Bundesliga match: Bayern Munich v VfB Stuttgart, Friday 28 August, 19:30 (BST)

The age-old question is as relevant as ever after Vincent Kompany's side cruised to a domestic double last season while playing some truly scintillating football.

Harry Kane is 33 now but is showing no signs of slowing down - the England captain has scored 98 goals in 94 Bundesliga games and has broken countless records.

While questions may be asked of 40-year-old goalkeeper Manuel Neuer and his unconvincing backline, Bayern's devastating firepower of Kane, Michael Olise and Luis Diaz, plus the addition of Morocco international Ismael Saibari, means they should easily outscore their opponents.

Borussia Dortmund, RB Leipzig and Bayer Leverkusen are all capable of launching title challenges, but tend to come unstuck against stubborn mid-table sides.

Elsewhere, fallen giants Schalke 04 are looking to re-establish themselves as a top flight side after three years away. Their promotion heralds the return of one of the fiercest derbies in world football - the Revier derby against Dortmund.

Elversberg were playing in the regionalised fourth tier as recently as 2021-22, but secured promotion to the Bundesliga for the first time in their history to complete a fairytale rise.

With a population of about 13,000, Spiesen-Elversberg will be the smallest town to be represented in the Bundesliga. The odds are stacked against them.

Kane set for talks with Bayern Munich over new deal

Ex-Man City striker Dzeko, 40, pens new Schalke deal

First Ligue 1 match: Marseille v Strasbourg, Friday 21 August, 19:45 (BST)

It is hard to see anything other than Paris St-Germain winning Ligue 1 for the 13th time in 15 seasons, especially off the back of back-to-back Champions League triumphs.

That said, Luis Enrique's side can be got at - last season they lost six league games, two more than in the previous two campaigns combined.

PSG have added attacking midfielder Maghnes Akliouche from Monaco and Aston Villa left-back Lucas Digne to their star-studded squad this summer, but could end up selling wingers Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye amid interest from Liverpool.

Monaco (2016-17) and Lille (2020-21) are the two most recent sides to topple the Parisians, but neither looks equipped to do so again.

Financial difficulties have limited traditional heavyweights Marseille in the transfer market, with more key players set to follow Mason Greenwood out of the club.

Will Still (Auxerre) and Liam Rosenior (Paris FC) are back in the league after ill-fated managerial spells in England, while former Brazil full-back Felipe Luis has been installed as Monaco boss.

Lens were PSG's closest challengers last season, but may need time to bed-in new manager Dino Toppmoller. Lille, who finished third, face a similar situation with Davide Ancelotti.

Strasbourg have been a team on the up in recent years, but after losing manager Rosenior and then Gary O'Neil to the Premier League, face another restart under the relatively inexperienced Hugo Oliveira.

After losing the spine of the team that reached the Uefa Conference League semi-finals last season, the Alsace side have suffered some heavy defeats in pre-season.

Pogba expected to have Monaco contract terminated

Digne completes move to PSG from Aston Villa

Plenty of big names have joined Turkish clubs in recent years, but Mohamed Salah signing for Trabzonspor came as a surprise.

After leaving Liverpool at the end of his contract, Salah decided to join the 2021-22 Super Lig champions rather than one of Turkey's big three - Galatasaray, Fenerbahce and Besiktas. He'll be remembered as a hero if he can deliver a title at the first time of asking.

In the Netherlands, PSV Eindhoven are looking to win a fourth successive Eredivisie title.

Ajax and Feyenoord are looking to bounce back from disappointing campaigns having since appointed new managers - Spaniard Michel at Ajax and former Netherlands captain Giovanni van Bronckhorst in Rotterdam.

Porto are looking to successfully defend a Primeira Liga title for the first time since 2013, but will surely be challenged by Clasico rivals Benfica, now under the management of Marco Silva.

Sporting CP are looking to reclaim the title after winning it in 2023-24 and 2024-25.

The Eredivisie and Primeira Liga are already under way, while the Turkish Super Lig begins on Friday, 14 August with Galatasaray v Corum (19:30 BST).
